t: Module 1 Training Lab 0: Document Standards
x: Module 1 Training Lab 0: Document Standards training lab 1.0 Document Standards Module 1: Threat Intelligence & Reconnaissance Overview Welcome to NEXUS Security Consulting. Before you touch a client engagement, you need to be able to produce a document that holds together. Every Engagement Packet you submit this term is graded partly on mechanics: whether your Table of Contents is accurate, whether your figures are numbered and referenced, whether your sources are cited. Those points were the single largest avoidable loss last term, and none of them had anything to do with security knowledge. This lab teaches the mechanics once, on a sandbox document you cannot break in any way that matters, and then tests them on a quiz you can take as many times as you like. “Nobody outside this building sees your terminal. They see the report. I have watched excellent technical work get dismissed because the Table of Contents was full of screenshot filenames and half the figures were numbered by hand. Learn the tools once and you never think about it again.” Maya Rodriguez Senior Penetration Tester, NEXUS Security Assignment Objectives Confirm your computer can host the Kali VM that every later lab depends on Diagnose the document faults that cost the most points on Engagement Packets Repair each fault with Word’s built-in tools instead of manual formatting Verify a packet is clean before you submit it, using the Navigation Pane and a full field update Key Concepts Heading styles, and what the Table of Contents actually collects Automatic figure captions and cross-references Word’s citation manager and the reference list it builds for you Document properties as your identity on a file check_circle This Lab Stands On Its Own Nothing you do in Lab 1.0 is submitted, graded by hand, or folded into anything later. The practice document is yours to keep or throw away, and your grade comes entirely from the Canvas quiz. You are learning the tools here so that they are already familiar when the graded work starts. That is the whole purpose of this lab, and it ends when the quiz does. warning The Easiest 100 You Will Get: Take It Lab 1.0 is one of ten Training Labs and you do get one drop. Do not spend it here. The quiz allows unlimited attempts and every wrong answer returns an explanation, so there is no version of this where you cannot reach 100. Everything on it reappears on five Engagement Packets, where the points are not free. lightbulb Desktop Word Only, and Do Not Pay for It Use desktop Microsoft Word, Windows or Mac. Word for the web cannot create the captions, cross-references and citation fields this lab is about, and neither can Google Docs. Do not buy Word, and do not pay for a Microsoft 365 subscription. Office Professional Plus is free for all UTSA students and installs on up to five personal devices. Go to portal.office.com , sign in with your first.last@my.utsa.edu address, click the waffle icon in the top-left, choose Office 365, then Install Office > Office 365 apps . Activate with your abc123@utsa.edu credentials and your UTSA passphrase. Full details: UTSA Tech Solutions: Office Professional Plus for Students . If you are stuck getting it installed, post in #module-1-help before you spend a cent. time guide Estimated completion times per checkpoint Task Est. Time Checkpoint 1: Pre-flight hardware check and captures 10 min Checkpoint 2: Open the sandbox and turn on the Navigation Pane 5-10 min Checkpoint 3: Read the four right/wrong pairs 10-15 min Checkpoint 4: Repair the five planted faults 15-25 min Checkpoint 5: Update every field and verify 5-10 min Checkpoint 6: Set your document identity 5 min Checkpoint 7: Take the Lab 1.0 quiz 10-15 min Total Estimated Time 55-85 min These times are a guide, not a requirement. There is nothing to log and nothing to report. Take as long as you need. checkpoint 1 Pre-Flight: Can Your Machine Run This Course? What You’re Doing Checking four things about the computer you intend to use this term: how much memory it has, how much free disk it has, what kind of processor it has, and whether virtualization is switched on. Why It Matters Lab 1.1 asks you to build a Kali Linux virtual machine, and every lab after it runs inside that VM. If your machine cannot host one, you need to know in week 1 while there is still time to do something about it, not the night Lab 1.1 is due. This takes five minutes and it is the only part of this lab that is about hardware. Check your memory. Windows: Task Manager > Performance > Memory. Mac: Apple menu > About This Mac. Check your free disk space. Windows: Settings > System > Storage. Mac: Apple menu > System Settings > General > Storage. Check your processor type. Windows: Task Manager > Performance > CPU, or Settings > System > About. Mac: About This Mac. Look for ‘Chip: Apple M1/M2/M3/M4’ versus ‘Processor: Intel’. This determines which Kali image you download, so do not skip it. Windows only: confirm virtualization is enabled. Task Manager > Performance > CPU. Look for ‘Virtualization: Enabled’ on the right. If it says Disabled, it has to be turned on in your BIOS/UEFI before any hypervisor can run a VM at all. Search the web for “enable virtualization” plus your computer’s make and model : the key you press at boot (often F2, F10, Del or Esc) and the name of the setting (VT-x, AMD-V, SVM Mode, Intel Virtualization Technology) both differ by manufacturer, so there is no single instruction that covers everyone. Take a screenshot of each check. Windows: press Windows + Shift + S and drag a box around the panel. The snip goes to your clipboard, and a notification appears in the bottom-right. Click it, then press Ctrl + S to save the file. If that feels fiddly, press Windows + PrtScn instead: it grabs the whole screen and writes a .png straight into Pictures > Screenshots with nothing further to do. Mac: press Command + Shift + 4, then drag a box around the panel. The .png lands on your Desktop by itself. Command + Shift + 3 grabs the whole screen if you would rather not aim. Confirm you have four saved files, not four clipboard copies. This is the step people skip. A snip sitting on the clipboard disappears the moment you copy anything else, and Insert > Pictures needs a file on disk. Give them names you will recognize: memory, disk, processor, virtualization. Write the four answers down. If any of them fall short, act on it today (see below). What Lab 1.1 Will Ask For Item What Lab 1.1 needs If you fall short Memory The Kali VM is allocated 4096 MB minimum, 8192 MB recommended. Your machine has to run that and your normal desktop at the same time. 8 GB total is workable at the 4096 MB setting. Below that, talk to me in week 1. Free disk An 80 GB virtual disk (dynamically allocated, so it grows as you use it) plus a ~4 GB Kali ISO download. Dynamic allocation means it will not claim 80 GB on day one, but it grows all term. If you are tight on space, clear room now rather than mid-engagement. Processor The Kali image has to match your processor: amd64 for Intel/AMD, arm64 for Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4). This is true whichever hypervisor you use. Get the architecture right before you download anything. The image is roughly 4 GB and the wrong one will not boot. Virtualization Enabled in BIOS/UEFI. Windows machines frequently ship with it off. It is a BIOS setting, not a Windows setting. Search for “enable virtualization” plus your make and model. The boot key and the setting’s name vary by manufacturer. If you are not comfortable changing BIOS settings, post in #module-1-help and we will walk through it. warning Apple Silicon Users: Check Before You Download If About This Mac says Chip: Apple M1, M2, M3 or M4, you are on ARM and you need the arm64 Kali image, not the amd64 one. That is about the processor, not the hypervisor. It holds no matter what you run the VM in. The download is roughly 4 GB, so it is a slow mistake to make twice. warning If Your Machine Does Not Clear This Bar, Tell Me in Week 1 Post in #module-1-help now. Not in week three. There are options (adjusting the VM allocation, campus lab machines, other arrangements), but every one of them takes time to sort out, and none of them work well the night before a deadline. A machine that cannot run the VM is a solvable problem in week 1 and a serious one in week 4. check_circle What You Should Have Four known numbers (your memory, your free disk, your processor type, and, on Windows, whether virtualization is enabled), plus a screenshot of each one saved where you can find it again. And if any of them are short, a message already posted in #module-1-help. lightbulb Use the Hypervisor That Fits Your Computer This course doesn’t pick your hypervisor for you. In Lab 1.1 you describe your computer to the AI assistant you use, it recommends the best fit from a list of options (most are free), and then it tailors the setup steps to the one you choose. What is graded is the outcome: a working Kali VM that meets the Lab 1.1 requirements, named <your abc123>, and the evidence you are asked to capture. checkpoint 2 Open the Sandbox and Turn On the Navigation Pane What You’re Doing Downloading the Lab 1.0 sandbox document, opening it in desktop Word, and turning on the one panel that tells you whether your document is healthy. Why It Matters The Navigation Pane and the Table of Contents read from the same source: heading styles. Anything wrong in the Pane will be wrong in the Table of Contents. Keeping it open while you work is the difference between catching a problem in ten seconds and hunting it for an hour. lightbulb Download the Sandbox IS3513_Lab1.0_Sandbox.docx . Open it in desktop Word. Nothing you do to this file is submitted or graded. Break it on purpose. Download the sandbox document: IS3513_Lab1.0_Sandbox.docx. Save it somewhere you can find it again. Open it in desktop Microsoft Word. Not a browser, not Google Docs, not Preview. Maximize the Word window. In a narrow window Word collapses the ribbon to unlabelled icons and every instruction below becomes a scavenger hunt. Turn on the Navigation Pane. Windows: View > Navigation Pane (tick the checkbox). Mac: View > Sidebar > Navigation. Leave it open for the whole lab. check_circle What You Should Have The sandbox open in desktop Word with a panel down the left side listing the document’s sections. You should be able to click an entry and jump to it. warning Common Pitfalls If the sandbox opens in Protected View, click Enable Editing. You cannot change styles until you do. Mac users: the Navigation Pane is called the Sidebar, and it has several modes. You want Navigation, not Thumbnails or Find. If you do not have desktop Word, get it now through your UTSA account. Do not start Lab 1.1 without it. checkpoint 3 Read the Four Pairs What You’re Doing Reading through the sandbox’s demonstration section, where each of the four mechanics appears twice: once done correctly and once done the way that costs points. Why It Matters You are not being asked to memorize rules in the abstract. Each pair puts the right way and the wrong way next to each other so you can see the difference in the document itself, and in the Navigation Pane, rather than being told about it. Scroll to Appendix B: Additional Screenshots. The four pairs live there. Pair 1, Captions. Compare the correct caption against the one styled as Heading 2. Watch the Navigation Pane as you scroll past them. Only one of them shows up as a section. Pair 2, The blank heading. Find the blank entry in the Navigation Pane. There is an empty paragraph carrying a heading style, and it is invisible in the document body. Pair 3, Cross-references. One says Figure 1 because Word computed it. The other says Figure 1 because somebody typed it. They look identical right now. Pair 4, Citations. Same story: one is a field, one is text. Click each one. The real citation highlights gray when you click it; typed text does not. lightbulb Pro Tip Clicking is t

t: Module 1 Training Lab 1: Kali Environment Setup › Overview
x: training lab 1.1 Kali Environment Setup Module 1: Threat Intelligence & Reconnaissance Overview Welcome to NEXUS Security Consulting. In this foundational lab, you will deploy your personal security operations platform using Kali Linux in a virtualized environment. This setup will serve as your primary workspace for all hands-on exercises throughout the semester. You'll learn to configure virtual machines, install Docker for containerized client targets, and verify your environment is ready for purple team operations. “Every analyst at NEXUS starts here: building their own lab environment. This isn't just homework; it's your personal security workstation. Treat it like your toolkit. You'll use this setup for every client engagement this semester. Document everything. Your future self will thank you when you're writing runbooks at 2 AM.” Maya Rodriguez Senior Penetration Tester, NEXUS Security Chapters Covered Chapter 1: Introduction to Security | Chapter 2: General Security Concepts Client Context Brazos Financial Group : Dallas-based wealth management firm ($2.8B AUM, 450 employees) facing an SEC cybersecurity examination in six months. Your Module 1 engagement begins with internal training: you'll build the analyst workstation and toolkit you'll use for the Brazos network reconnaissance assessment in Unit 3. Assignment Objectives Deploy Kali Linux as your security operations platform Install and verify Docker for containerized client targets Document your environment for your Module 1 Engagement Packet Key Concepts Virtualization fundamentals and hypervisor architecture Kali Linux as a purpose-built security testing platform Docker container fundamentals and container vs. VM differences Environment verification and baseline documentation lightbulb Use the Hypervisor That Fits Your Computer This course doesn’t tell you which hypervisor to use. Your computer decides that. Checkpoint 1 gives you the requirements your Kali VM has to meet and the options with what they cost. You describe your computer to the AI assistant you use, it recommends the best fit, and then it tailors the setup steps to the hypervisor you choose. That is a real use of AI: turning a general spec into steps for your own machine. What is graded is the outcome: a working Kali VM that meets the requirements, named with your abc123, and the evidence you’re asked to capture. warning Technically Droppable, Actually Required Lab 1.1 is one of ten Training Labs, and you do get one drop. So administratively, yes, you could skip this one and have it not count against your grade. But practically, you can’t skip it. Lab 1.2 needs your Kali VM running. So do EP 1, Labs 2.1, 2.2, every lab through Module 5. Skip Lab 1.1 and you’ll have to come back and do it anyway before Lab 1.2 is due , except now your drop is gone and the deadline is tighter. Use your drop on a lab that doesn’t gate everything that follows it. folder Save For EP 1 This is Unit 1 of a 3-unit module. Create a folder called Module1_Screenshots and save EVERY screenshot there. You'll compile these into your Module 1 Engagement Packet in Unit 3. schedule Time Guide Task Est. Time Checkpoint 1: Choose and install your hypervisor 20-30 min Checkpoint 2: Download Kali Linux ISO 20-45 min Checkpoint 3: Create and configure VM 10-15 min Checkpoint 4: Install Kali Linux 20-30 min Checkpoint 5: Install and verify Docker 10-15 min Checkpoint 6: System verification 10-15 min Total Estimated Time 85-140 min This is Unit 1 of 3. Log these hours as Internal Training on your EP 1 timesheet. Save every screenshot to your Module1_Screenshots folder. You’ll need them all in Unit 3. Next: CP1 →

t: Module 1 Training Lab 1: Kali Environment Setup › CP1: Choose and Install Your Hypervisor
x: checkpoint 1 Choose and Install Your Hypervisor Choosing the hypervisor that fits your computer, with an AI assistant’s help, and installing it. Why It Matters Virtual machines allow you to run a complete operating system inside your existing OS. This is how security professionals maintain isolated environments for testing tools, malware analysis, and client engagements without risking their primary system. warning Your Computer Comes First The Information Systems and Cybersecurity department requires you to own a laptop that meets its minimum device requirements . Every lab in this course runs on the VM you build here, so check your computer against that page before you start. If you don’t have access to a suitable machine, start with the options on that page, including the one-time financial aid adjustment for technology, and email me right away at john.newsom@utsa.edu so we can get you sorted as soon as possible. Don’t wait until the lab is due. error What Your VM Has to Be Whichever hypervisor you use, your Kali VM has to meet every one of these. They are the same for everyone. Kali image: the official installer for your processor: amd64 for Intel or AMD, arm64 for Apple silicon (Checkpoint 2). Memory: 4 GB minimum, 8 GB recommended if your computer can spare it. Processor cores: 2 or more. Disk: 80 GB, dynamically allocated (it grows as it fills). OS type, if your hypervisor asks: Linux, Debian 64-bit (ARM64 on Apple silicon). Networking: NAT. Parallels and UTM call it Shared Network. VM name and hostname: your abc123. Kali account: username kali , password kali (Checkpoint 4). lightbulb No Preference? Use the Defaults If you don’t care which tools you use, don’t spend time deciding: use Microsoft Copilot (free with your UTSA account) and VirtualBox (free). Still run the Find the right setup prompt and take Screenshot 01. If the answer says VirtualBox won’t run on your computer, go with what it recommends instead. Pick Your AI Assistant Assistant Cost Worth knowing Microsoft Copilot (UTSA) Free with your UTSA account UTSA turns it on for every student 18 or older. Sign in at copilot.microsoft.com with your @my.utsa.edu address and passphrase. Signed in, it has Microsoft’s enterprise data protection, so what you type isn’t used to train the AI. Details: utsa.edu/techsolutions/FacAndStaff/AI-Literacy/copilot-chat.html ChatGPT Free tier; paid plans available Sign up at chatgpt.com. Claude Free tier; paid plans available Sign up at claude.ai. Gemini Free tier; paid plans available Sign in with a Google account at gemini.google.com. Each name links to the assistant’s own site. The free tier of any of these is plenty for this course. If you don’t have a favorite, start with Copilot. Pick Your Hypervisor Hypervisor Runs on Cost Worth knowing VirtualBox Windows, Linux, Mac Free Does not run Kali on a MacBook Neo. VMware Workstation / Fusion Workstation: Windows, Linux. Fusion: Mac Free for personal and educational use The download needs a free Broadcom account, and Broadcom offers no support for the free version. Parallels Desktop Mac Paid subscription, 50% off for students Runs on every Apple silicon Mac, including the MacBook Neo. The Standard edition caps a VM at 8 GB of memory and 4 cores. UTM Mac Free from its website ($9.99 in the Mac App Store) Built on QEMU. Hyper-V Windows Pro, Education or Enterprise Included with Windows Not available on Windows Home. Each name links to its official download page (Hyper-V is built into Windows, so its link shows how to turn it on). Prices and support change. Check the official page before you pay for anything. Pick your AI assistant from the table above (no preference: Copilot). It’s the one you’ll paste the AI Assist prompts into, on this lab and the rest. Find your computer’s specs: operating system and version, processor, memory and free disk space. Windows: Settings > System > About, and Settings > System > Storage for free space. Mac: Apple menu > About This Mac, and System Settings > General > Storage for free space. Copy the Find the right setup prompt from the AI Assist card below into the AI assistant you use, fill in your specs and your budget, and send it. Check it against the source of truth. Open the sources the AI listed and the hypervisor’s official page, and confirm three things yourself: it runs on your processor and operating system, what it costs, and that it can meet every requirement in What Your VM Has to Be . Where the AI and the official page disagree, the official page wins. Take Screenshot 01 (below) before you move on. Install the hypervisor you chose, using its official instructions. Kali keeps a guide for running Kali in each one: kali.org/docs/virtualization . Open it to confirm it runs. lightbulb Trust the Source, Not the AI An AI answer is a summary of what it has read, and it can be out of date or simply wrong while sounding completely sure. Prices change, supported chips change, menus get renamed. The source of truth is the original: the vendor’s official page, the tool’s documentation or man page, the standard itself, and in this course, the lab sheet. So use AI to get pointed in the right direction and to understand what you’re reading, then read the source and go by what it says. This is a habit analysts live by: nothing goes in a report because an AI said so, only because you checked it. In your EP 1 Runbook VM setup entry, next to Screenshot 01, name the official page you checked and anything the AI got wrong. That’s also the kind of example the AI Methodology Reflection asks for. warning Getting Unstuck Your hypervisor, your computer, your setup. There are too many combinations of hardware, operating systems and hypervisors for anyone to support them all, so setup problems are yours to solve, and AI is your first tool for solving them. That isn’t me being difficult. You have me for one semester, and after that you’ll be handed unfamiliar systems with nobody to ask, so start the habit now: when you’re stuck, ask an AI. Use the Decode my error prompt below: paste the exact error, say what you were doing, and tell it your setup. If the first answer doesn’t fix it, tell the AI what happened when you tried it and keep going. Still stuck after a real effort? Post the error and what you’ve tried in #module-1-help on Discord. Someone with the same setup may have already solved it. Capture photo_camera 01-hypervisor-recommendation.png Capture your AI conversation showing the prompt with your computer’s specs and the AI’s recommendation. Your VM doesn’t exist yet, so this one is the exception to the abc123 rule. Save as 01-hypervisor-recommendation.png. It goes in your EP 1 Runbook, in the entry for your VM setup. What You Should Have A hypervisor installed and opening on your computer, an AI’s recommendation for your computer saved as Screenshot 01 and checked against the official page, and your choice ready to report on the Lab 1.1 quiz. warning Common Pitfalls smart_toy AI Assist menu_book Textbook Reference search Dig Deeper warning Taking the AI’s word for it: if the recommendation says a hypervisor is free or supports your chip, confirm it on the official page before you install anything. Describing your computer vaguely: an AI can only fit the recommendation to the computer you describe. “A laptop” gets you a generic answer. Windows on ARM (Snapdragon) is the hard case: support for running Kali there is limited. Give the AI your exact processor and Windows edition, and expect it to point you to the arm64 image. Virtualization turned off: if no hypervisor will start a VM, virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V) has to be turned on in your BIOS/UEFI. Lab 1.0 shows how to check. macOS blocking the install: allow the hypervisor in System Settings > Privacy & Security. smart_toy Use AI on this lab. These prompts are good ways to get more out of this checkpoint: copy one into the AI you use (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot or another) and fill in anything in [brackets]. No favorite yet? UTSA gives every student Microsoft Copilot free: sign in at copilot.microsoft.com with your @my.utsa.edu address. The free tier of any of them is plenty. They ask the AI to teach you, not to do the work for you. This sheet is still the spec: if the AI’s commands or wording differ from it, follow the sheet. Why It Matters Kali Linux comes pre-loaded with hundreds of security tools. A proper installation ensures all tools work correctly and the system is stable for the entire semester. t: Module 1 Training Lab 1: Kali Environment Setup › CP5: Install and Verify Docker
x: checkpoint 5 Install and Verify Docker Installing Docker, the containerization platform we'll use to deploy vulnerable lab targets throughout the course. Why It Matters Docker lets us spin up isolated, vulnerable systems safely. Each module's client engagement uses Docker containers. Without it, you can't complete the labs. Update your package lists sudo apt update What this does Concept: apt update refreshes the list of available packages from the repositories. It does not install anything. It just checks what's available. Always run this before installing new software so you get the latest versions. Upgrade all installed packages to current versions sudo apt full-upgrade -y What this does Concept: full-upgrade installs the newest versions of everything already on the system. Kali is a rolling release, so your ISO is a snapshot frozen at build time. This step brings your tools up to current. Use full-upgrade rather than plain upgrade: full-upgrade is allowed to add or remove packages to resolve dependency changes, so nothing gets held back. This is why your tool versions will match what the labs and quizzes expect. Install Docker and Docker Compose sudo apt install -y docker.io docker-compose What this does Concept: apt install downloads and installs packages. The -y flag automatically answers "yes" to the confirmation prompt. docker.io is the container engine; docker-compose lets you define multi-container environments in a single file. Enable Docker to start automatically and start it now sudo systemctl enable docker --now What this does Concept: systemctl enable tells the system to start Docker automatically on every boot. The --now flag also starts it immediately so you don't have to reboot first. Add your user to the Docker group sudo usermod -aG docker $USER What this does Concept: usermod -aG appends your user to a group. By default, Docker commands require root access. Adding yourself to the docker group lets you run Docker without sudo every time. Log out of Kali and log back in (or reboot the VM) so the group change takes effect What this does Concept: Your group memberships are read when you log in, so the terminal you already have open does not know you joined the docker group. Until you log out and back in, Docker commands without sudo fail with a permission error. Check the Docker version docker --version What this does In your output: You should see the installed Docker version number. If you get "command not found", the installation didn't complete correctly. Run the Docker test container docker run hello-world What this does Concept: docker run pulls an image from Docker Hub and runs it as a container. The hello-world image is a tiny test container that prints a success message. If you see "Hello from Docker!", Docker is fully working. In your output: You should see "Hello from Docker!" followed by a short explanation of what Docker just did. If you get "permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket", you haven't logged out and back in since adding yourself to the docker group. Do that, then run this command again. t: Module 1 Training Lab 1: Kali Environment Setup › CP6: System Verification
x: checkpoint 6 System Verification Running a series of commands to verify your environment is properly configured and all required tools are available. Why It Matters Catching configuration issues now prevents frustration later. A working baseline environment means you can focus on learning security concepts instead of troubleshooting setup problems. Part A: System Information Display your hostname hostname What this does In your output: This should show your abc123 (for example, aaa000). If it shows kali, the word abc123, or any name that isn’t your ID, fix it before proceeding. Display kernel and OS information uname -a What this does Concept: uname -a prints all system information: kernel name, hostname, kernel version, architecture. The -a flag means "all." This is a standard first step when documenting an engagement environment. Part B: Network Connectivity Display your network interfaces and IP addresses ip addr What this does Concept: ip addr lists all network interfaces and their assigned IP addresses. Look for your eth0 interface. It should have an IP address from your hypervisor’s NAT network (the range depends on the hypervisor; VirtualBox uses 10.0.2.x). Test internet connectivity ping -c 3 8.8.8.8 What this does Concept: ping sends ICMP echo requests to test network reachability. The -c 3 flag limits it to 3 packets. 8.8.8.8 is Google's public DNS. If all 3 packets come back, you have internet connectivity. Part C: Security Tools Verify Nmap is installed nmap --version What this does Concept: Nmap is the industry-standard network scanner. t: Module 1 Training Lab 2: Reconnaissance Tool Exploration › CP1: nmap Network Scanning
x: checkpoint 1 nmap Network Scanning Demonstrating network scanning fundamentals using nmap against authorized targets. You'll perform version detection and script scanning to identify services and potential vulnerabilities. Why It Matters Nmap is the industry-standard network scanner. Understanding its capabilities helps both attackers (who use it to map target networks) and defenders (who need to understand what attackers see). Version detection reveals exactly what software is running, which directly informs vulnerability research. Open a terminal in your Kali VM Run a version detection scan: nmap -sV scanme.nmap.org What this does Concept: The -sV flag tells Nmap to probe open ports and determine what service and version is running on each one. Without it, Nmap only tells you a port is open. With it, you learn what software is listening (for example, the name and version of the web server or SSH server). In your output: Look for the VERSION column in the results table. Each open port should show specific software and version numbers. This information is what makes vulnerability research possible. Check the first line of the report too. The address in parentheses after scanme.nmap.org should not start with 127. If it does, your network’s DNS is sending you back to your own machine and you are scanning your own VM, which is why every port shows closed. Look up the real address with dig +short scanme.nmap.org @8.8.8.8 and scan that address instead. Note the open ports and service versions detected Run a default script scan: nmap -sC scanme.nmap.org What this does Concept: The -sC flag runs Nmap’s default set of scripts against discovered services. These scripts perform safe enumeration tasks like grabbing SSH host keys, checking HTTP headers, and detecting common misconfigurations. In your output: Compare this to the -sV output. You should see additional details like SSH host keys and HTTP page titles that weren’t in the version scan. Scripts extend Nmap from a port scanner into an information-gathering platform. Compare the output. What additional information did scripts reveal? terminal Key Flags -sV: Version detection -sC: Default scripts -A: Aggressive (combines -sV, -sC, OS detection, traceroute) Capture photo_camera 08-nmap-version.png Capture nmap -sV results. Save as 08-nmap-version.png photo_camera 09-nmap-scripts.png Capture nmap -sC results. t: Module 1 Training Lab 2: Reconnaissance Tool Exploration › CP2: netcat Banner Grabbing
x: checkpoint 2 netcat Banner Grabbing Using netcat to manually connect to network services and capture their identification banners: the text services display when you connect. Why It Matters Service banners reveal software versions, hostnames, and configuration details. This low-level technique helps verify nmap results and often reveals information automated scanners miss. Netcat is the “Swiss Army knife” of networking. Connect to SSH port on scanme.nmap.org: nc -v scanme.nmap.org 22 What this does Concept: nc (netcat) opens a raw TCP connection to a host and port. The -v flag enables verbose output so you can see the connection status. Port 22 is the standard SSH port. In your output: You should see a connection message followed by the SSH banner (a line starting with SSH-2.0- followed by the server software and its version). This banner reveals the exact software version. That is valuable intel for an attacker. Observe the banner that appears (SSH version string) Press Ctrl+C to disconnect Try connecting to port 80: nc -v scanme.nmap.org 80 What this does Concept: Port 80 is the standard HTTP port. Unlike SSH, web servers don’t send a banner automatically. You need to send an HTTP request first. This teaches you that different protocols behave differently during reconnaissance. In your output: You’ll see a connection confirmation, but no banner yet. You need to type the HTTP request in the next step to get a response. Type HEAD / HTTP/1.0 and press Enter twice to get HTTP headers What this does Concept: HEAD / HTTP/1.0 is a raw HTTP request asking the server for headers only (no page content). The response reveals the web server software, version, and sometimes OS details. This is manual banner grabbing for HTTP, exactly what automated tools do behind the scenes. x: checkpoint 3 dirb Directory Discovery Using dirb to brute-force discover hidden directories and files on web servers, finding content that isn’t linked from the main site. Why It Matters Web apps often have hidden admin panels, backup files, or development directories. Directory brute-forcing finds these resources that attackers commonly exploit. lightbulb Your Target: the NEXUS Training Range Checkpoints 3 and 4 scan the NEXUS training range, a practice web server that runs on your own VM using the Docker you installed in Lab 1.1. Start it with the first step below. It keeps running until you stop it, so Checkpoint 4 uses the same one. The range hands back a real mix of response codes: some paths return 200, some 403, and missing ones 404. Read its robots.txt too. Start the NEXUS training range on your VM: docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name nexus-range jfnewsom/nexus-range:latest What this does Concept: -d runs the container in the background, -p 8080:80 makes its web server answer on port 8080 of your VM, and --name gives it a name you can stop it by. Run docker ps and confirm nexus-range shows as Up before you scan. Run dirb against the range: dirb http://127.0.0.1:8080 What this does Concept: dirb sends HTTP requests for thousands of common directory and file names (from a wordlist) and reports which ones exist. It’s a brute-force approach to content discovery: finding pages the site doesn’t link to publicly. In your output: Watch for lines showing CODE:200 (the page exists) versus CODE:403 (forbidden but exists) and CODE:301 (redirect). Each discovered path is a potential attack surface. Watch it test common directory names Note which return CODE:200 (found) Let it run or press Ctrl+C after several results terminal Wordlist Location Default wordlists: /usr/share/dirb/wordlists/ Capture photo_camera 11-dirb-results.png Capture dirb output showing discovered directories. Save as 11-dirb-results.png What You Should Have Output showing discovered directories like /admin/, /images/, /cgi-bin/ with HTTP response codes. If you used the NEXUS range instead, expect a mix of accessible and forbidden paths: several directories returning CODE:200, several returning CODE:403, and a robots.txt worth reading. A 403 is a finding, not a failure. It confirms the path is really there, which is exactly what a 404 does not tell you. warning Common Pitfalls smart_toy AI Assist menu_book Textbook Reference search Dig Deeper warning Forgetting http://: URL must include the protocol (dirb http://target, not just dirb target) Slow scan: Dirb tests thousands of paths; use Ctrl+C after seeing results for training purposes Connection errors: Target site must be reachable; test with curl first if dirb fails smart_toy Use AI on this lab. t: Module 1 Training Lab 2: Reconnaissance Tool Exploration › CP4: nikto Vulnerability Scanning
x: checkpoint 4 nikto Vulnerability Scanning Using nikto to scan web servers for known vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and dangerous files. Why It Matters Nikto checks for 6,700+ dangerous files and 1,250+ outdated server versions. It quickly identifies low-hanging fruit that attackers commonly exploit. lightbulb Same Target as Checkpoint 3 nikto scans the NEXUS training range you started in Checkpoint 3. If you rebooted or stopped it since, start it again with docker start nexus-range and confirm with docker ps . When nikto finishes, stop and remove the range: docker stop nexus-range , then docker rm nexus-range . Run nikto against the range: nikto -h http://127.0.0.1:8080 What this does Concept: nikto is a web server vulnerability scanner that checks for thousands of known issues: outdated software, dangerous default files, misconfigurations, and insecure headers. The -h flag specifies the target host. In your output: Each line prefixed with + is a finding. Look for server version disclosures, missing security headers, and OSVDB reference numbers. These findings would go into a real vulnerability assessment report. Watch the output: nikto reports findings as it scans Note types of findings: server info, outdated software, dangerous files Let it run for a few minutes Capture photo_camera 12-nikto-results.png Capture nikto output showing findings. Save as 12-nikto-results.png What You Should Have Output showing server information, potential vulnerabilities, and interesting files discovered. If you used the NEXUS range instead, expect findings in the same categories: a disclosed server version, a missing security header, a directory with indexing left enabled, and entries in robots.txt flagged for manual review. warning Common Pitfalls smart_toy AI Assist menu_book Textbook Reference search Dig Deeper warning Wrong port: Use -p 443 for HTTPS targets; nikto defaults to port 80 Loud scanning: Nikto is NOT stealthy; every request is logged and easily detected False positives: Verify findings manually; nikto reports potential issues, not confirmed vulnerabilities smart_toy Use AI on this lab. t: Module 1 Training Lab 2: Reconnaissance Tool Exploration › CP5: enum4linux SMB Enumeration
x: checkpoint 5 enum4linux SMB Enumeration Exploring enum4linux capabilities for SMB/Windows enumeration. Since we don’t have a live SMB target, you’ll review the tool’s help output and understand its purpose. Why It Matters SMB (Server Message Block) is ubiquitous in Windows networks. Enum4linux extracts usernames, shares, group memberships, and password policies. That is critical information for both attackers and security assessments. You’ll use this tool against the Brazos Financial container next unit. Review enum4linux help: enum4linux -h What this does Concept: enum4linux is a tool for enumerating information from Windows/Samba systems using the SMB protocol. The -h flag displays all available options. We’re reviewing the help now because you’ll use this tool against a live target in EP 1. In your output: Focus on the flags listed in the Key Flags callout below. Each flag extracts a different type of information from Windows systems: usernames, file shares, password policies, and group memberships. Note the different enumeration options (-U for users, -S for shares, etc.) Understand what each flag discovers terminal Key Flags -U: Get user list -S: Get share list -P: Get password policy -a: Do all simple enumeration Capture photo_camera 13-enum4linux-help.png Capture enum4linux help output. t: Module 1 Training Lab 2: Reconnaissance Tool Exploration › CP6: searchsploit Vulnerability Research
x: checkpoint 6 searchsploit Vulnerability Research Using searchsploit to search the Exploit Database for known vulnerabilities and exploits based on software versions discovered during reconnaissance. Why It Matters Once you know what software a target runs, you need to research whether known exploits exist. Searchsploit provides offline access to Exploit-DB, the largest public archive of exploits and vulnerable software. Update the database: sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade exploitdb What this does Concept: Searchsploit works offline by searching a local copy of the Exploit Database, which Kali installs as the exploitdb package. Upgrading that package pulls in the latest exploits. New vulnerabilities are published daily, so keeping this current matters. You may see sudo searchsploit -u used for this elsewhere. It updates the same database, but on a fresh Kali install it can also download a separate 2.5 GB archive of papers that this lab does not use. Search for Apache vulnerabilities: searchsploit apache 2.4 What this does Concept: This searches the local Exploit-DB for any exploit matching “apache 2.4.” In a real engagement, you’d take the exact version from your Nmap scan (the server name and version number) and search for known exploits targeting it. This is where reconnaissance becomes actionable. In your output: You’ll see a table of matching exploits with titles, types (local, remote, webapps, DoS), and file paths. The path column tells you where the exploit code lives on your system if you need to examine it. Note the exploit titles, types, and paths Try searching for OpenSSH: searchsploit openssh What this does In your output: Compare the results to your Apache search. Notice the different exploit types and how the version numbers in the titles help you narrow down which exploits apply to a specific target. In practice, you’d cross-reference these results with the exact version string from your Nmap scan. Capture photo_camera 14-searchsploit-apache.png Capture searchsploit results for Apache. Save as 14-searchsploit-apache.png What You Should Have Search results showing exploit titles, paths, and platforms for Apache and OpenSSH. warning Common Pitfalls smart_toy AI Assist menu_book Textbook Reference search Dig Deeper warning Too broad: “apache” returns thousands; add version numbers to narrow results Outdated database: Run sudo apt install --only-upgrade exploitdb periodically to update Not all exploits work: Many require specific conditions; read the exploit code before attempting smart_toy Use AI on this lab. t: Module 1 Training Lab 2: Reconnaissance Tool Exploration › Purple
x: purple team Both Sides of the Shield security What Red Team Learns Reconnaissance is the Foundation: Every engagement starts with information gathering. nmap gives you open ports and versions; netcat confirms banners manually; dirb finds hidden paths; nikto flags known misconfigurations. Together, these six tools build a complete picture of a target’s attack surface. Version Intelligence Drives Exploitation: A version string from nmap or netcat banner grabbing feeds directly into searchsploit. A server name and version number becomes a CVE list. This chain (discover, identify, research) is the core offensive workflow. SMB Is a Username Factory: enum4linux null session enumeration extracts usernames, shares, and password policies without authenticating. That user list becomes your credential attack target. security What Blue Team Learns Your Logs Record This Reconnaissance: Every nmap scan, dirb request, and nikto probe leaves traces in access logs. Defenders who run these tools against their own infrastructure know exactly what a scan looks like and can build detection rules accordingly. Version Banners Are Information Leaks: Service banners reveal software versions to anyone who connects. Suppressing banners and obscuring version strings reduces the reconnaissance value an attacker gains from a scan. Authorized Scanning Is Blue Team Work: Running these tools on your own infrastructure before an attacker does is called attack surface management. Everything you discover today, a defender should already know about their own environment. sync_alt The Purple Team Connection The six tools in this lab are used identically by both sides. Red team runs them offensively to map targets. Blue team runs them defensively to audit their own exposure. The difference is authorization and intent, not the tools themselves. ← Back: CP6 Next: Wrap-up →

t: Module 1 Engagement Packet: Brazos Financial Reconnaissance Engagement › CP2: Deploy Brazos Container
x: checkpoint 2 Deploy Brazos Container Deploying the Brazos Financial Docker container that simulates their external attack surface. This is your authorized target for the engagement. Why It Matters Real penetration tests begin with scope definition and authorized target deployment. The Brazos container represents their actual exposed services: the same ports and configurations an external attacker would see. Pull the Brazos container image: docker pull jfnewsom/brazos-financial:latest What this does Concept: docker pull downloads a container image from Docker Hub. This image contains Brazos Financial’s simulated environment: a pre-configured system with intentional vulnerabilities for you to discover. The :latest tag ensures you get the current version. Run the container with all required ports: docker run -d -p 80:80 -p 443:443 -p 22:22 -p 139:139 -p 445:445 -p 137:137/udp -p 8443:8443 --name brazos jfnewsom/brazos-financial:latest What this does Concept: docker run creates and starts a container. The -d flag runs it in the background (detached). Each -p flag maps a container port to your host: 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 22 (SSH), 139 and 445 (SMB file sharing), 137/udp (the NetBIOS name service that goes with SMB), and 8443 (alternate HTTPS). These are the services you’ll scan: Brazos Financial’s exposed attack surface. Verify the container is running: docker ps What this does In your output: You should see a table with the brazos container listed as “Up.” Verify all seven port mappings appear in the PORTS column. If the STATUS shows “Exited,” the container crashed. Check the Common Pitfalls below. Then give the container about 30 seconds to finish starting before you scan it. Scan too soon and nmap shows every port as tcpwrapped with no versions. Note the container IP (usually localhost or 127.0.0.1) Capture photo_camera 15-brazos-container.png Capture docker ps showing Brazos container running. Save as 15-brazos-container.png What You Should Have Running Brazos container with all ports accessible at localhost. t: Module 1 Engagement Packet: Brazos Financial Reconnaissance Engagement › CP3: Full Reconnaissance Workflow
x: checkpoint 3 Full Reconnaissance Workflow Conducting comprehensive reconnaissance against the Brazos Financial container using all six tools from your training: nmap, netcat, dirb, nikto, enum4linux, and searchsploit. Why It Matters This is the core of your engagement. A thorough reconnaissance reveals everything an attacker would discover about Brazos Financial’s external attack surface. Your findings drive the entire client report. Run comprehensive nmap scan: nmap -sV -sC -A localhost What this does Concept: This combines all three Nmap techniques from Lab 1.2: version detection (-sV), default scripts (-sC), and aggressive mode (-A adds OS detection and traceroute). This is your primary reconnaissance scan. Document every open port, service, and version in your report. Perform banner grabbing with netcat on discovered ports Run dirb against the web services: dirb http://localhost What this does Concept: Brute-forces directory names on Brazos Financial’s web server. Look for admin panels, backup files, or configuration directories that shouldn’t be publicly accessible. Each finding is a potential vulnerability for your report. Execute nikto vulnerability scan: nikto -h http://localhost What this does Concept: Scans Brazos Financial’s web server for known misconfigurations, outdated software, and dangerous files. The findings from nikto complement your dirb results: nikto checks for specific vulnerabilities while dirb discovers hidden paths. Enumerate SMB with enum4linux: enum4linux -a localhost What this does Concept: The -a flag runs all enumeration checks: users, shares, groups, password policies, OS info. In Lab 1.2 you reviewed the help. Now you’re running it for real against Brazos Financial’s SMB service on port 445. Document any discovered usernames, file shares, or policy weaknesses. Research vulnerabilities for discovered versions using searchsploit Document ALL findings with screenshots Capture photo_camera 16-brazos-nmap-full.png Capture your full nmap scan against the Brazos target. The command and the complete results table must both be visible, showing open ports with service names and version strings. Save as 16-brazos-nmap-full.png photo_camera 17-brazos-netcat-banner.png Capture a netcat connection to one of the ports nmap found. The banner the service returns must be readable in the output, not just the connection line. x: purple team Both Sides of the Shield security What Red Team Learns Open ports and service versions are your attack blueprint. Banner grabbing reveals exact software without triggering IDS. Directory discovery exposes admin panels and backup files that defenders forgot existed. SMB enumeration hands you a username list for credential attacks, before you’ve touched a single login form. security What Blue Team Learns Your recon results are a defender’s punch list. Suppress version banners. Close ports that shouldn’t be public. Require authentication on SMB shares. Monitor for nmap, dirb, and nikto signatures in your logs. If you ran these tools undetected, so can an attacker. sync_alt The Purple Team Connection Brazos Financial’s legacy systems and poor configuration hygiene are blue team failures that created every finding in your report. x: training lab 2.1 Cryptographic Foundations Module 2: Cryptography & Authentication Overview This unit begins your cryptography training at NEXUS Security. You’ll master the fundamental cryptographic operations that underpin modern security: hashing for integrity verification, symmetric encryption for data protection, asymmetric encryption for secure key exchange, and digital signatures for non-repudiation. These skills prepare you for the Gulf Coast Healthcare engagement in Unit 3, where you’ll remediate certificate issues on their patient portal. “Cryptography isn’t magic. It’s math. And math done wrong is worse than no math at all because it gives false confidence. Every healthcare organization I’ve audited had encryption somewhere. Most had it implemented incorrectly. This unit, you’ll learn to do it right.” Maria Delgado, PhD Security Compliance Specialist, NEXUS Security Chapters Covered Chapter 6: Applied Cryptography | Chapter 11: Authentication and Remote Access Client Context Gulf Coast Healthcare Partners : Houston-based regional healthcare network (3 hospitals, 15 clinics, 2.1M patient records) rebuilding after a ransomware incident 18 months ago. This unit is internal training on cryptographic primitives and hash analysis; in Unit 3 you'll assess Gulf Coast's patient portal cryptography before their OCR audit. Assignment Objectives Generate and compare cryptographic hashes using SHA-256 Encrypt and decrypt files using AES symmetric encryption Generate RSA keypairs and perform asymmetric encryption Create and verify digital signatures Document all operations for your Module 2 Engagement Packet Key Concepts Cryptographic Hashing: SHA-256 and the avalanche effect: how small input changes produce completely different outputs, forming the foundation of data integrity verification. Symmetric Encryption: AES-256-CBC encryption and decryption, the standard healthcare organizations use to protect PHI at rest. Asymmetric Encryption: RSA keypair generation and public-key encryption, solving the key distribution problem that symmetric encryption cannot. Digital Signatures: Creating and verifying signatures using RSA, providing non-repudiation, the cryptographic proof that a specific party signed a specific document. Algorithm Deprecation: Why MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer acceptable: understanding collision resistance and NIST recommendations for current practice. Documentation for Auditors: Every screenshot and command output is evidence. t: Module 2 Training Lab 1: Cryptographic Foundations › CP1: Hash Functions
x: checkpoint 1 Hash Functions Generating cryptographic hashes using SHA-256 and demonstrating the avalanche effect: how small input changes produce completely different outputs. Why It Matters Hashes are the foundation of data integrity. Every time you verify a software download, check file integrity, or validate a digital signature, you’re using hashes. In healthcare, hash verification proves that patient records haven’t been tampered with, which is critical for audit trails and legal compliance. “Auditors don’t care what you did. They care what you can prove you did. Hash verification is how you prove data integrity.” Maria Delgado, PhD Security Compliance Specialist, NEXUS Security Part A: Create a test file and generate its hash Create a working directory: mkdir -p ~/lab2-crypto Change into your working directory: cd ~/lab2-crypto Create a sample patient record file: echo "Patient: John Smith, DOB: 1985-03-15, MRN: 12345" > patient.txt Generate the SHA-256 hash: sha256sum patient.txt What this does Concept: sha256sum computes a SHA-256 cryptographic hash: a fixed-length, 64-character hexadecimal fingerprint of a file. The same input always produces the same hash, but even a one-bit change produces a completely different output. This is how you prove a file has not been tampered with. In your output: You should see a 64-character hex string followed by the filename. This hash is unique to your file’s exact contents. Copy it somewhere. You’ll compare it in the next step. Part B: Demonstrate the avalanche effect Create a slightly modified file (change one character): echo "Patient: John Smith, DOB: 1985-03-16, MRN: 12345" > patient2.txt Compare the hashes: sha256sum patient.txt patient2.txt What this does In your output: Compare the two hashes carefully. Despite changing only one character, the hashes are completely different. This is the avalanche effect , a critical property of cryptographic hash functions. If small changes produced similar hashes, attackers could predict modifications. The avalanche effect makes that impossible. t: Module 2 Training Lab 1: Cryptographic Foundations › CP2: Symmetric Encryption
x: checkpoint 2 Symmetric Encryption Encrypting and decrypting files using AES-256, the symmetric encryption standard healthcare organizations use to protect patient health information (PHI) at rest. Why It Matters Symmetric encryption is how organizations protect bulk data. Every encrypted database, every secure file transfer, every protected backup uses symmetric encryption. AES-256 specifically is the gold standard. It’s approved for classified government information and the algorithm healthcare auditors expect to see. “Under HIPAA, you encrypt PHI at rest or you document why you didn’t. Auditors will ask. AES-256 is the standard. Know it cold.” Maria Delgado, PhD Security Compliance Specialist, NEXUS Security Part A: Encrypt a file with AES-256 Encrypt your patient file (use password nexus2026 when prompted): openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -pbkdf2 -in patient.txt -out patient.txt.enc What this does Concept: This encrypts a file using AES-256 in CBC mode, the same algorithm the U.S. government uses for classified information. Symmetric encryption means the same password both encrypts and decrypts. HIPAA doesn’t name an algorithm, but AES-256 is what auditors expect to see protecting patient health information (PHI) at rest. In your output: OpenSSL will prompt for a password twice (enter and verify). Use nexus2026 as instructed. No output means success. OpenSSL is silent on success. Flags: enc : Tells OpenSSL to perform encryption/decryption -aes-256-cbc : Algorithm: AES with 256-bit key in Cipher Block Chaining mode -salt : Adds random data so the same password + file produces different ciphertext each time -pbkdf2 : Uses PBKDF2 key derivation, which makes brute-force password attacks much slower -in / -out : Input plaintext file and output encrypted file Verify the encrypted file exists: ls -la patient.txt* View the encrypted contents as a hex dump: xxd patient.txt.enc | head What this does Concept: xxd is a hex dump utility that shows raw file bytes in hexadecimal format. Piping to head limits output to the first 10 lines. This lets you visually confirm the file is encrypted. You should see random-looking hex values, not readable text. In your output: The hex dump should show no recognizable text, just seemingly random bytes. The first 16 bytes contain the Salted__ header followed by the salt value. If you can read any of the original patient data, encryption failed. Part B: Decrypt the file Decrypt using the same password: openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -d -pbkdf2 -in patient.txt.enc -out patient_decrypted.txt What this does Concept: The -d flag switches OpenSSL to decrypt mode. This single flag reverses the encryption operation. Everything else stays the same: same algorithm, same key derivation. This demonstrates that symmetric encryption is reversible with the correct password. View the decrypted file: cat patient_decrypted.txt Confirm it matches the original: diff patient.txt patient_decrypted.txt && echo 'Files match!' || echo 'Files differ!' Capture photo_camera 03-symmetric-encrypt.png Capture the encryption command and the hex dump showing unreadable encrypted content. Save as 03-symmetric-encrypt.png photo_camera 04-symmetric-decrypt.png Capture the decryption and verification showing the original content restored. Save as 04-symmetric-decrypt.png What You Should Have Two screenshots showing successful encryption (unreadable ciphertext) and decryption (original plaintext restored). warning Common Pitfalls smart_toy AI Assist menu_book Textbook Reference search Dig Deeper warning Forgetting the password: Symmetric encryption requires the same password for decryption Using weak algorithms: DES is obsolete; always use AES-256 Missing -pbkdf2 flag: without it, OpenSSL falls back to an old, weak way of turning your password into a key and prints a deprecation warning. Decrypt with the same flags you encrypted with, or you get a bad decrypt error smart_toy Use AI on this lab. t: Module 2 Training Lab 1: Cryptographic Foundations › CP3: Asymmetric Encryption
x: checkpoint 3 Asymmetric Encryption Generating an RSA keypair and using it to encrypt and decrypt data. Unlike symmetric encryption (one shared key), asymmetric uses two mathematically related keys: a public key anyone can use to encrypt, and a private key only you possess to decrypt. Why It Matters Asymmetric encryption solves the key distribution problem. How do you securely share a symmetric key with someone you’ve never met? You use their public key. This is how TLS/HTTPS works, how secure email works, and how certificates establish trust. “Encryption is not magic. It’s math. And math done wrong is worse than no math at all. It gives false confidence.” Maria Delgado, PhD Security Compliance Specialist, NEXUS Security Part A: Generate an RSA keypair Generate a 2048-bit RSA private key: openssl genrsa -out private.pem 2048 What this does Concept: This generates an RSA private key, the mathematical foundation for asymmetric cryptography. Unlike symmetric encryption (one shared secret), RSA uses a keypair: a private key you guard with your life, and a public key you share freely. The security comes from how hard it is to factor a very large number back into the two prime numbers that were multiplied to make it. Flags: genrsa : Generate an RSA private key -out private.pem : Save to PEM format (Base64-encoded, human-readable headers) 2048 : Key size in bits. NIST minimum for RSA. 4096 is more future-proof but slower. Extract the public key: openssl rsa -in private.pem -pubout -out public.pem What this does Concept: The public key is mathematically derived from the private key, but the reverse is computationally infeasible. This one-way relationship is what makes asymmetric crypto work: you can freely distribute your public key without exposing your private key. Anyone with your public key can encrypt messages that only your private key can decrypt. List both key files: ls -la *.pem View the public key contents: cat public.pem Part B: Encrypt with public key Create a small message to encrypt: echo "Secret: AES key is nexus2026" > secret.txt Encrypt with the public key: openssl pkeyutl -encrypt -pubin -inkey public.pem -in secret.txt -out secret.enc What this does Concept: Public key encryption: anyone with your public key can encrypt a message, but only the private key holder can decrypt it. This solves the key distribution problem: you never need to share a secret password over an insecure channel. Flags: pkeyutl : Public key utility for encrypt/decrypt/sign/verify operations -encrypt : Perform encryption (use -decrypt to reverse) -pubin : Input key is a public key (not a private key) -inkey : Path to the key file to use Verify the encrypted file exists: ls -la secret.enc What this does Concept: pkeyutl prints nothing when it succeeds, so list the file to confirm it was written. RSA output is always the size of the key, so a 2048-bit key produces a 256-byte file no matter how short the message was. Part C: Decrypt with private key Decrypt using the private key: openssl pkeyutl -decrypt -inkey private.pem -in secret.enc -out secret_decrypted.txt Verify the decrypted contents: cat secret_decrypted.txt Capture photo_camera 05-rsa-keypair.png Capture the keypair generation, file listing, and public key contents. Save as 05-rsa-keypair.png photo_camera 06-rsa-encrypt.png Capture the encryption command and verify the encrypted file exists. Save as 06-rsa-encrypt.png photo_camera 07-rsa-decrypt.png Capture the decryption showing the original secret message restored. Save as 07-rsa-decrypt.png What You Should Have Three screenshots showing keypair generation, public key encryption, and private key decryption. warning Common Pitfalls smart_toy AI Assist menu_book Textbook Reference search Dig Deeper warning Confusing public/private: Encrypt with public, decrypt with private (for confidentiality) Data size limits: RSA can only encrypt small amounts of data directly Exposing private key: Never share or commit private keys smart_toy Use AI on this lab. t: Module 2 Training Lab 1: Cryptographic Foundations › CP4: Digital Signatures
x: checkpoint 4 Digital Signatures Creating and verifying digital signatures using RSA. Digital signatures use the private key to sign (proving authenticity) and the public key to verify (confirming identity). It uses the keys the opposite way from encryption. Why It Matters Digital signatures provide non-repudiation: proof that a specific person signed a specific document. In healthcare, this is legally binding. When a physician signs an order electronically, that signature must be verifiable and undeniable. “Non-repudiation matters in healthcare. When a provider signs an order, it’s legally binding.” Maria Delgado, PhD Security Compliance Specialist, NEXUS Security Part A: Sign a document Create a document to sign: echo "Medication Order: Amoxicillin 500mg TID x 10 days - Dr. Chen" > order.txt Sign with your private key: openssl dgst -sha256 -sign private.pem -out order.sig order.txt What this does Concept: Signing uses the keys the opposite way from encryption. You sign with your private key, and anyone can verify with your public key. This provides non-repudiation : proof that a specific person signed a specific document. In healthcare, this is how electronic prescriptions and medical orders are legally binding. Flags: dgst : Message digest (hash) operations -sha256 : Hash the document with SHA-256 before signing -sign private.pem : Sign using your private key; only you can create this signature -out order.sig : Save the binary signature to a separate file Verify the signature file was created: ls -la order.* Part B: Verify the signature Verify using the public key: openssl dgst -sha256 -verify public.pem -signature order.sig order.txt What this does In your output: You should see Verified OK . This confirms three things simultaneously: (1) the document has not been modified since signing, (2) the signature was created by the holder of the matching private key, and (3) the signer cannot deny having signed it (non-repudiation). If even one byte of order.txt changed, verification would fail. Capture photo_camera 08-signature-create.png Capture the signing command and file listing showing both the order and signature files. x: purple team Both Sides of the Shield security What Red Team Learns Hash Collision Exploitation: Hash collisions expose weak integrity checks: with MD5 or SHA-1, an attacker can craft two different files that share one hash, such as a harmless document and a malicious one, and swap one for the other without the hash check noticing. Symmetric Key Theft: Intercepting or stealing AES keys gives full decryption capability; key management failures are more common than algorithm breaks. RSA Key Misuse: Confusing public and private key roles, or using undersized keys, allows attackers to break encryption or forge signatures on affected systems. security What Blue Team Learns Hash Algorithm Policy: Use SHA-256 or stronger for all integrity checks; flag any system still using MD5 or SHA-1 as a compliance finding. Key Management Controls: Enforce key management policies: keys stored at rest must be encrypted, and private keys must never leave the system that generated them. Signature Verification: Verify digital signatures as part of software deployment pipelines. Unsigned or unverified binaries are a malware delivery vector. sync_alt The Purple Team Connection You generated keys and signed documents as a builder this unit. In Module 4 you will reverse that perspective, analyzing how attackers exploit weak key management and deprecated algorithms to compromise the same systems you are securing here. ← Back: CP4 Next: Wrap-up →

t: Module 2 Training Lab 2: Authentication Systems › CP1: SSH Key Generation
x: checkpoint 1 SSH Key Generation Generating SSH keypairs using both RSA and ED25519 algorithms. You’ll compare the two key types and understand when to use each. Why It Matters SSH key authentication is the industry standard for secure remote access. Unlike passwords, keys are cryptographically strong, can’t be guessed through brute force, and provide non-repudiation. Every server you’ll manage in your career will use key-based authentication. “ED25519 is the modern choice: smaller keys, faster operations, strong security. But you’ll still see RSA everywhere. Know both.” Derek Mitchell Blue Team Lead, NEXUS Security Part A: Generate an RSA keypair Create a working directory for this lab: mkdir -p ~/lab2-auth Change into your working directory: cd ~/lab2-auth Generate a 4096-bit RSA key (press Enter for defaults, use passphrase nexus2026 ): ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -f ./id_rsa_lab -C "lab-rsa-key" What this does Concept: ssh-keygen generates SSH keypairs for passwordless authentication. Like the RSA keys from Lab 2.1, SSH keys use asymmetric cryptography, but formatted for the SSH protocol. The private key stays on your machine; the public key goes on any server you want to access. In your output: You’ll see a randomart image, a visual fingerprint of your key. Two files are created: id_rsa_lab (private, keep secret) and id_rsa_lab.pub (public, safe to share). Flags: -t rsa : Key type: RSA (the classic, widely compatible algorithm) -b 4096 : Key size: 4096 bits (double the NIST minimum for stronger security) -f ./id_rsa_lab : Output file path (avoids overwriting your real SSH keys) -C "lab-rsa-key" : Comment embedded in the key, which helps identify which key is which on servers with many authorized keys List the generated files: ls -la id_rsa* View the public key contents: cat id_rsa_lab.pub Part B: Generate an ED25519 keypair Generate an ED25519 key (modern, faster, smaller; use passphrase nexus2026 again): ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./id_ed25519_lab -C "lab-ed25519-key" What this does Concept: ED25519 is a modern elliptic curve algorithm that provides security comparable to RSA-3072 with much smaller keys and faster operations. Most security professionals now recommend ED25519 for new deployments: shorter keys, faster math, no known weaknesses. You’ll still encounter RSA on legacy systems, which is why you learned both. List all key files: ls -la id_* Compare the key sizes: wc -c id_rsa_lab.pub id_ed25519_lab.pub What this does In your output: wc -c counts bytes in each file. The RSA public key will be roughly 750 bytes while ED25519 is about 100 bytes, yet they provide comparable security. Smaller is better when security is equal. t: Module 2 Training Lab 2: Authentication Systems › CP2: Key Permissions
x: checkpoint 2 Key Permissions Understanding and configuring proper file permissions for SSH keys. You’ll see why SSH refuses to use keys with incorrect permissions and how to fix common permission problems. Why It Matters A private key with world-readable permissions is a security disaster. SSH clients will refuse to use improperly secured keys, and attackers specifically look for misconfigured key files. Proper permissions are the difference between security and breach. Part A: Examine default permissions Check the current permissions on your keys: ls -la ~/lab2-auth/id_* What this does Concept: In Linux, every file has three permission groups: Owner, Group, and Others. Each group gets three bits: r (read=4), w (write=2), x (execute=1). Add them up per group to get octal notation. Private keys should be 600 ( -rw------- ), public keys 644 ( -rw-r--r-- ), and the ~/.ssh directory 700 ( drwx------ ). In your output: You should see -rw------- for private keys and -rw-r--r-- for public keys. The first column is the permission string. View the same permissions in octal notation: stat -c '%a %n' ~/lab2-auth/id_* What this does In your output: Private keys should show 600 and public keys 644 , confirming what ls -la showed. These are the correct, SSH-enforced permission levels. Part B: Demonstrate the risk of weak permissions Copy the private key to a shared directory for this demonstration: cp ~/lab2-auth/id_ed25519_lab /tmp/demo_key What this does Concept: Your home directory ( /home/ followed by your username) has permissions 700 , so other users can’t enter it. /tmp is world-readable and world-writable, which is realistic: in enterprise environments, files often end up in shared directories like /tmp or /var/www . In those locations, file permissions are your only line of defense . Make the copy world-readable (INSECURE; for demonstration only): chmod 644 /tmp/demo_key What this does Concept: You’re changing this key from 600 (owner read/write only) to 644 (owner read/write, group can read, others can read). The permissions change from -rw------- to -rw-r--r-- . That r-- at the end means every user on this machine can now read this file: fine for public keys, a disaster for private keys. Prove it: read the key as a completely different user: sudo -u nobody cat /tmp/demo_key What this does Concept: sudo -u nobody runs the following command as the nobody account: a minimal, unprivileged account with no special access to your files. Think of it as a stand-in for any random user or compromised process on this machine. In your output: You should see the entire private key printed to your terminal, starting with -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY----- . This is the actual cryptographic secret. Anyone who has this data can impersonate you on any system where this key is authorized. Part C: Fix the permissions and verify Restrict the file back to owner-only: chmod 600 /tmp/demo_key What this does Concept: chmod 600 sets permissions to -rw------- : 6 = read+write for owner, 0 = nothing for group, 0 = nothing for others. The change takes effect immediately. The kernel enforces it on the very next access attempt. Try reading the key as nobody again: sudo -u nobody cat /tmp/demo_key What this does In your output: You should now see: cat: /tmp/demo_key: Permission denied . Same command, same user, same file. Only three digits changed (644 → 600). This is the principle of least privilege in action. Clean up the demo file: rm /tmp/demo_key What this does Concept: Good security hygiene: don’t leave copies of sensitive material in shared directories, even in a lab. Confirm your original keys still have correct permissions: stat -c '%a %n' ~/lab2-auth/id_* What this does In your output: Private keys should show 600 and public keys 644 . t: Module 2 Training Lab 2: Authentication Systems › CP3: SSH Configuration
x: checkpoint 3 SSH Configuration Setting up SSH infrastructure: the authorized_keys file that controls who can connect, the SSH config file that simplifies connections, and testing key-based authentication to localhost. Why It Matters Understanding SSH configuration is essential for any security professional. The authorized_keys file is your access control list: every public key there can authenticate. The config file lets you manage connections to dozens of servers efficiently. Gulf Coast uses this exact setup for their infrastructure. “Never rely on a single control. Layer your defenses so one failure doesn’t mean total compromise. SSH config files let you enforce security policies across all your connections.” Derek Mitchell Blue Team Lead, NEXUS Security Part A: Set up authorized_keys Create the .ssh directory if it doesn’t exist: mkdir -p ~/.ssh Set secure directory permissions: chmod 700 ~/.ssh Add your public key to authorized_keys : cat ~/lab2-auth/id_ed25519_lab.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys What this does Concept: The authorized_keys file is an access control list: every public key listed there can authenticate as this user. The >> operator appends rather than overwrites, preserving existing keys. This is how SSH key-based auth works: your client offers a private key, the server checks if the matching public key is in authorized_keys , and if so, grants access without a password. Set secure file permissions: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Verify the directory contents: ls -la ~/.ssh/ Confirm the authorized key: cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys Part B: Test key-based authentication Stop the Brazos container from EP 1 if it is still running. It holds port 22, and SSH to localhost would reach Brazos instead of your VM: docker stop brazos What this does Concept: Brazos published its SSH port as 22, the same port your Kali SSH server needs. If you rebooted since EP 1, Brazos is already stopped and this just prints its name. If you see No such container , there is nothing to stop. Start the SSH service if not running: sudo systemctl start ssh Verify SSH is running: sudo systemctl status ssh Connect to localhost using your key: ssh -o PasswordAuthentication=no -i ~/lab2-auth/id_ed25519_lab localhost whoami What this does Concept: Adding a command after the hostname ( whoami ) tells SSH to run that single command on the remote system and return the output, instead of opening an interactive shell. This is how automated scripts and CI/CD pipelines use SSH. SSH will ask for your key’s passphrase (nexus2026) first. That is the key file unlocking on your own machine, and it is expected. The prompt you should not see is your Kali account password ( yourname@localhost’s password: ). In your output: The first time, SSH asks Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? Type yes ; it is your own machine. Then it asks for your key passphrase (nexus2026). That unlocks the key on your machine; it is not a password. You should see your username and no prompt for your account password. Flags: -o PasswordAuthentication=no : Disables password fallback so the connection only succeeds with the key -i : Specifies which private key to use (identity file) Part C: Create an SSH config file Open a new config file in nano: nano ~/.ssh/config What this does Concept: nano is a simple terminal-based text editor. The commands at the bottom use ^ to mean the Ctrl key, so ^O means Ctrl+O . Since the file doesn’t exist yet, nano will create it when you save. Type or paste the following contents, replacing YOUR-USERNAME with your own Kali username (run whoami if you’re not sure). Use spaces, not tabs, for indentation: Host labserver HostName localhost User YOUR-USERNAME IdentityFile ~/lab2-auth/id_ed25519_lab IdentitiesOnly yes What this does Concept: Host labserver : the alias you’ll type. HostName localhost : the actual server address. User YOUR-USERNAME : the account to log in as. It must match your Kali username exactly; if it doesn’t, SSH tries to log in as a user that doesn’t exist on your VM. IdentityFile : which private key to use. IdentitiesOnly yes : only try the specified key, preventing SSH from cycling through all keys in ~/.ssh/ . Save and exit nano: press Ctrl+O , then Enter to confirm the filename, then Ctrl+X to exit. Lock down config file permissions: chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config What this does Concept: Your SSH config contains key paths and server details. Setting 600 ensures only you can read or modify it, the same protection level as your private keys. Verify the config file contents: cat ~/.ssh/config Test the connection using your alias: ssh labserver whoami What this does Concept: The alias pulls the hostname, user and key from your config file, so this is the same login as Part B in fewer keystrokes. Expect the same key passphrase prompt as before, and no account password prompt. Capture photo_camera 14-authorized-keys.png Capture the .ssh directory listing and authorized_keys content. Save as 14-authorized-keys.png photo_camera 15-ssh-keyauth.png Capture the successful SSH connection using key-based authentication. Save as 15-ssh-keyauth.png photo_camera 16-ssh-config.png Capture the SSH config file contents and successful connection using the alias. Save as 16-ssh-config.png What You Should Have Three screenshots showing authorized_keys setup, successful key-based SSH connection, and SSH config file usage. You should be able to connect with only your key passphrase, never your account password. warning Common Pitfalls smart_toy AI Assist menu_book Textbook Reference search Dig Deeper warning Wrong key in authorized_keys: Make sure you’re adding the .pub file, not the private key Line breaks in key: The public key must be all on one line Config layout: Put each setting on its own line under Host , indented with spaces, not tabs. If everything is on one line, SSH never sees the HostName and fails with Could not resolve hostname labserver . Run cat ~/.ssh/config to check the file. Wrong username in config: The User line must match your own Kali username, not kali unless that’s the name you chose at setup.
