t: Engagement Packet Guide
x: engagement packet guide Two Audiences, One Document, Every Module Every module ends with an Engagement Packet — the work product that wraps up your client engagement. A real security engagement produces two distinct artifacts: documentation that stays inside the firm, and a deliverable that goes to the client. Your Engagement Packet mirrors that reality. One .docx file submitted to Canvas, two parts inside it: Part I Internal Part II Client Weighting 40 / 60 Format .docx groups The audience rule Part I is for us. Part II is for them. The client never sees Part I — your timesheet, your runbook, your reflection on the engagement. That’s NEXUS internal documentation. The client only sees Part II — the Client Deliverable. Anything you’d be embarrassed to show the client (“I got stuck for two hours on this nmap flag,” “ChatGPT helped me figure out what the error meant”) belongs in Part I, not Part II. Keep the audience boundary clean and your writing becomes a lot easier. task_alt Required for every Engagement Packet Submitted as .docx from desktop Microsoft Word (Windows or Mac) — no PDFs, no Google Docs, and not Word for the web , which cannot produce the fields this packet requires. At least 20 qualifying screenshots from your module's labs , each inline next to the text that references it, with your abc123 visible in the terminal prompt or in the title bar of the full Kali VM window. 10+ references meeting the source quality standard — see the Citations page. Both Part I and Part II must be present — a missing part is graded zero for that part. schedule Deadline Tip Submit at least 10 minutes before the deadline , even if the packet isn’t perfect. Canvas accepts unlimited submissions until the deadline hits — you can keep uploading better versions right up to the cutoff. A 70 beats a zero every time. Start Here: Download & Set Up the Template Don’t format an Engagement Packet by hand. Download the NEXUS template and fill it in — the cover, both parts, every section heading, the Table of Contents and the reference list are already built. The template carries structure only: headings, tables, and bracketed slots you type over. Nothing in it is an example, so nothing in it can be shipped to a client by accident. The worked examples are further down this page, where you can read them safely. Two things you set once, and they fill in everywhere. The cover meta-table, the running header, and the title all read from Word’s document properties, so you enter them a single time instead of typing them on every page: Client is already filled in. Each module’s template ships with that module’s client pre-set — you don’t enter it. Keep the structure. Don’t rename or reorder the sections. The grading script and the rubric both expect the headings exactly as they ship. Delete every remaining placeholder. Before you submit, search the document for an opening square bracket — Ctrl+F on Windows, ⌘F on Mac — and work through every hit. Anything still in brackets is scaffolding that was never meant to reach a reader. Delete any timesheet rows you did not use. 1. Open the template in DESKTOP Microsoft Word (Windows or Mac). Not Google Docs and not Word for the web — both break the fields and the auto Table of Contents. 2. Open document properties — File → Info (Windows) or File → Properties (Mac). Set two properties: • Author → your name • abc123 → your VM identifier (the custom property near the bottom of the properties list) 3. Your abc123 is your own UTSA ID (e.g. xqz947). It MUST match the <your abc123> hostname shown in your screenshots. It is the key we use to tie this packet to your VM. 4. Select all, then RIGHT-CLICK inside the selection and choose "Update all fields". This works the same on Windows and Mac. (Keyboard equivalent: Ctrl+A / Cmd+A then F9. On a Mac you may need fn+F9 if your function row is set to media controls.) This refreshes every field — cover, header, figure numbers, citations and the Table of Contents — so they show real values. 5. Do step 4 again as the LAST thing before you submit, so the Table of Contents page numbers are current. Download Your Template Every module has a ready-to-use template — cover page, both packet parts, all section headings, and an auto-generating Table of Contents already built. Pick your module: Module 1 Reconnaissance Brazos Financial ⬇ EP_M1_Brazos.docx Module 2 Cryptographic Assessment Gulf Coast Healthcare ⬇ EP_M2_GulfCoast.docx Module 3 Network Traffic Analysis Gulf Coast Healthcare ⬇ EP_M3_GulfCoast.docx Module 4 Password Security Alamo Industries ⬇ EP_M4_Password_Audit.docx Module 5 Risk & Vulnerability LoneStar DevOps ⬇ EP_M5_LoneStar.docx What Goes in Every Section A section-by-section map of the template. Part I is internal (NEXUS leadership and the next analyst); Part II is the client deliverable (Brazos leadership, mostly non-technical). Write each section for its audience. Part I · Timesheet: Log your hours across all three units, split Internal Training (Units 1–2) vs. Client Billable (Unit 3). Log one line per work session rather than one per unit, delete any rows you do not use, and total the columns yourself. Need more rows? Right-click inside the last row and choose Insert → Insert Rows Below. If you logged honestly as you went, this is a 10-minute fill-in. Part I · Runbook: A man-page style entry for each tool or step — purpose, switches, the exact command you ran, sample output, next steps, pitfalls. Test: could the next analyst reproduce your work from this alone? Pair each screenshot with the command that produced it. Part I · Analyst Reflection: Three honest prompts — a timesheet self-audit, a professional reflection, and the AI methodology reflection. No word floor. “I didn’t use AI (N/A)” is fine if it’s true. Part II · Executive Summary: One page maximum, board-readable. What you did, what you found, what to do — in plain language a non-technical executive can act on. Part II · Methodology: A high-level overview of scope, approach, and tools. Command-by-command detail belongs in your runbook, not here. Part II · Findings: Ordered highest severity first. Each finding keeps every field: number, title, severity, affected host/port, description, evidence (screenshot reference), impact, recommendation. Finding 003 in the template is your model. Part II · Risk Analysis: Likelihood × impact per finding, consistent with your severity labels. Part II · Recommendations: Prioritized — what to do this week vs. this quarter — each tied back to a finding number. Part II · Appendix: Raw (scrubbed) tool output, extra screenshots, and your references. Screenshots & References Screenshot naming: Use the ##-description.png convention (e.g. 07-nmap-service-scan.png) so they sort in order and are easy to reference. Screenshots: at least 20 qualifying screenshots per module earns full screenshot credit, and each one short of 20 is −2.5%. Your abc123 must be visible in every one: in the terminal prompt, or in the title bar of the full Kali VM window. More than 20 earns nothing on its own, but a screenshot that evidences a stretch goal is how that work gets credited. Where they go: Screenshots go inline, inside the .docx, next to the text that references them. Training Lab work (X.1 and X.2) goes in the Runbook, under the entry for the tool that produced it. Client work (the Engagement Packet) goes in Part II, with the finding, methodology step or appendix item it supports. If a runbook entry needs a client screenshot, point to it by figure number with a cross-reference instead of pasting it twice. A screenshot uploaded as a separate file, attached in Canvas or posted as a Canvas comment is not in the packet and does not count. Reference minimum: At least 10 properly-formatted references (−5% for each one below 10), and each one must be cited at least once in the body of the packet — bibliography-only entries do not count. CVE entries, vendor advisories, NIST publications, and tool documentation all count. The course textbook does not count toward the ten — it ships in the template as a formatting example, and you do not have to delete it. Use Word’s References tab → Insert Citation, then generate the bibliography — don’t hand-type it. Part I: The Internal Packet Part I is what NEXUS keeps in the engagement file. Three components, all internal: A. NEXUS Timesheet Audience: NEXUS leadership / billing. Where did your hours go? Hours broken out by unit, split between internal training (Units 1–2, non-billable) and client billable (Unit 3 fieldwork). Justify any unusually high or low hour count with a one-line note (“spent 4 hours debugging tool installation”). If you logged hours honestly as you went, this is a 10-minute fill-in. If you’re reconstructing it the night before, it’ll show — your scan dates, screenshot timestamps, and command history won’t line up with your claimed hours. The template includes a pre-built timesheet table; just fill in the cells. ✓ Good Example — Module 1 Timesheet A Module 1 (Brazos Financial) timesheet that gives leadership exactly what they need to bill the client and assess the engagement: WEEK 1 — Internal Training (4.0 hours) • Kali VM installation, hostname configured to <your abc123> ............... 1.5 hr • Hypervisor network configuration (NAT for the engagement) .... 0.5 hr • Lab 1.1 environment verification (uname -a, ip a, screenshot capture) .. 1.0 hr • Documentation setup (screenshot folder structure, runbook scaffolding) . 1.0 hr WEEK 2 — Internal Training (3.5 hours) • nmap deep dive: read man page, tested -sS / -sV / -O flags ............. 1.5 hr • dirb / nikto / enum4linux: practice runs against scanme.nmap.org ....... 1.0 hr • searchsploit workflow: paired CVE lookup with version output .......... 0.5 hr • Tool inventory documentation for runbook ............................. 0.5 hr WEEK 3 — Client Billable (6.0 hours) • Brazos Financial: full TCP scan, top-1000 ports ........................ 0.5 hr • Service version detection on open ports (-sV -sC --version-intensity 5) 1.0 hr • Web reconnaissance: dirb, nikto, manual inspection .................... 1.5 hr • SMB enumeration: enum4linux against discovered host ................... 0.5 hr • Vulnerability research: searchsploit + CVE lookups on discovered versions 1.5 hr • Client Deliverable: executive summary + 3 finding writeups + risk analysis 1.0 hr ENGAGEMENT TOTAL: 13.5 hours | Internal: 7.5 hr | Billable: 6.0 hr Why this works: Every line ties to a specific activity, command, or output Times are realistic and reflect actual effort — not all 30-min round numbers Internal vs. billable categories are clearly distinguished A billing manager could justify the 6 client-billable hours from the listed activities The total aligns with what your screenshot timestamps and command history would show ✗ Bad Example — Vague, Round-Number Timesheet A timesheet that fails the basic "could a manager bill the client from this" test: Unit 1 (3 hours) - Did the lab stuff - Set up VM Unit 2 (2 hours) - Practiced with tools - Took some screenshots Unit 3 (4 hours) - Scanned the client - Wrote report Total: 9 hours Why this fails: "Did the lab stuff" tells leadership nothing — there's no way to justify the hours to a client No breakdown by specific tools or commands Times are suspiciously round (3, 2, 4) — real engagement work isn't billed in whole-hour chunks No internal vs. billable distinction — leadership can't tell which hours go on the client invoice The total (9 hr) is implausibly low for a three-unit engagement — either you didn't do the work or didn't track it Would be rejected by any real consulting firm before reaching the client B. Internal Runbook Audience: The next analyst who has to do this engagement next month. If a colleague picked up this client next quarter, could they reproduce what you did from your runbook alone? Environment setup, tools you used (and which versions), the exact commands you ran, what the expected output looks like, and

t: GenAI Policy
x: genai policy Academic Integrity & AI Use psychology Are you here to learn this material, or are you here for a grade? Pick honestly. The rest of this policy depends on your answer. If you’re here to learn , AI is one of the most powerful tools you’ll ever have. Used right, it’s a force-multiplier — it’ll accelerate your understanding, sharpen your writing, and help you produce work you couldn’t produce alone. You will leave this course better at security work AND better at working with AI. Both, at the same time. If you’re here just for a grade , AI can technically do most of this course for you. The catch is that we both know how that ends. You’ll get the grade. You won’t have the skills. And when a recruiter asks you to walk through a vulnerability scan you “completed” in IS3513, or to run an Nmap command in a live technical interview, you’ll be staring at a terminal you’ve never actually used. That’s the moment that decides whether you get a security career or not — and AI can’t be in the room with you. help_outline The Question That Decides Everything Before you submit any work, ask yourself one question: “Will I be able to do this work at my first job — without asking AI for help?” If the answer is yes , you’ve used AI the right way. You learned something, validated it against your own knowledge, and produced work you can defend. If the answer is no , you probably won’t get that first job — and if you do, you won’t keep it. Interviews are how the industry filters out people who can’t do the work. AI can write you a great résumé. It can’t make you good at the live technical screen. Why Employers Care Before you even get to the job, you have to get through the interview. Security interviews include live technical screens — code-along tests, capture-the-flag exercises, hands-on lab challenges. Recruiters specifically design these to filter out candidates who can talk about security but can’t do it. You can’t bring ChatGPT to a Zoom interview where the panel is watching your screen. When you walk into your first cybersecurity job, your manager isn’t going to grade your work on a curve. They’re going to hand you a real problem with real stakes — a client’s network, a production system, an incident in progress — and expect you to know what to do. They’ll assume you actually learned what your transcript says you learned. In security work, your findings have to be defensible and reproducible . If you tell a client they have a critical vulnerability, you need to prove it with evidence from tools you actually ran. AI-generated fabrications create false positives that waste client money, false negatives that miss real threats, and either one will damage your professional reputation fast. The skills this course builds — running tools, interpreting output, documenting methodology, writing for clients — are exactly what employers and certifications test. AI accelerates the learning; it doesn’t replace it. ✓ Use AI Like This (you’re learning) Explaining command syntax — Ask what a flag does, then use it yourself Troubleshooting errors — Paste the error, get debugging help, verify the fix works Understanding concepts — Have AI explain an idea a different way until it clicks Proofreading & grammar — Refine your own writing for clarity Suggesting structure — Get feedback on how to organize what you’ve already written and analyzed ✗ Don’t Use AI Like This (you’re cheating yourself) Generating analysis you didn’t perform — AI cannot interpret your scan results for you Writing report sections that present findings as yours — Executive summaries, findings, and recommendations are your work product Answering quiz questions — Quizzes verify YOU did the hands-on work Completing labs without doing them — You must actually run the tools on your own VM Substituting AI predictions for real evidence — If AI tells you what a tool would output, that doesn’t replace running the tool Real Examples ✓ OK to Ask “What does the -sV flag do in Nmap?” “Why am I getting ‘permission denied’ when running this?” “How should I organize my findings section?” (you’ve done the analysis; you’re asking how to present it) “Is this paragraph clear?” (you wrote it; AI helps you refine it) ✗ Not OK to Ask “Write an executive summary for my Nmap scan” (the writing is your work product) “Generate a vulnerability assessment report” (the analysis is what you’re being assessed on) “What would Wireshark show if I captured DNS traffic?” (the answer is “go capture it and find out” — predicting tool output is how you avoid building the skill) school Tutor, Not Ghostwriter Think of AI like a tutor — someone who explains, demonstrates, and helps you think clearly. Not a ghostwriter who hands you finished work to put your name on. Tutors make you smarter. Ghostwriters make you fragile. AI in Engagement Packets Every Engagement Packet ends with one reflection question: where AI helped you, and how you validated what it told you . This isn’t a confession box — it’s how you build a record of working methodology over the term. Strong answers describe specific moments of help and the verification step that followed (e.g., “I asked Claude to explain ARP poisoning; I confirmed the explanation against the textbook chapter and the Ettercap documentation before writing my section.”). By Module 5, you should have a clear sense of where AI helps you and where it stops being useful. That’s the methodology employers want to see. summarize The Bottom Line The goal of this course is to make you a security professional with a working AI methodology — both at the same time . If you can defend the work as yours, AI helped you. If you can’t, it replaced you. Questions about what’s allowed? Ask in #course-questions on Discord, or email.

t: Grading Info
x: grading info How Your Work Is Evaluated Your grade reflects professional competency , not just completion. Engagement Packets are graded in three tiers: additive scoring for the quality of what you submitted (Tier 1), documentation deductions for missing requirements (Tier 2), and a small bonus for work that exceeds the spec (Tier 3). Category Weights Category Weight Components Training Labs 30% 10 Training Labs (quiz-verified) Engagement Packets 45% 5 Engagement Packets (manually graded) Module Exams 25% End-of-module exams (5 total) Engagement Packet Grading: Additive Scoring (Tier 1) Your Engagement Packet is graded across two parts, weighted 40/60. Each section has its own sub-weight and is graded on a qualitative scale specific to that section. See the published Grading Standard for the full per-section level descriptors. Part I — Internal Packet (40%) Section Weight What We Evaluate Timesheet 5% Hours by unit, split internal training vs. client billable, justified, aligned with screenshot timestamps. Runbook 20% Man-page style per-tool entries. Could the next analyst reproduce your engagement from this alone? Analyst Reflection 15% Honest, specific reflection. AI usage disclosed and validated, or N/A if not used. Part II — Client Deliverable (60%) Section Weight What We Evaluate Executive Summary 12% One page max. Risk posture, severity counts, top recommendations with business framing. Methodology 7% Brief client-facing narrative of your engagement approach. Findings 22% Numbered, severity-rated, evidence-backed findings ordered by severity. Risk Analysis 11% Per-finding likelihood and impact, reasoned through the client’s business context. Recommendations 8% Prioritized — Monday-morning fixes vs. next-quarter budget items. Cover Page, Table of Contents, and Appendix are mechanical requirements — they are either present or not, and their absence is handled in the Documentation Deductions section below. Documentation Deductions (Tier 2) −5% per missing reference (10 required, each cited in-text) −2.5% per qualifying screenshot short of 20 (20 qualifying screenshots per module earns full credit) −20% if the Appendix is missing −10% if the Executive Summary exceeds one page −5% if the Cover Page is missing −5% if the Table of Contents is missing or hand-typed −5% if Word fields aren’t updated (visible “Error! Reference source not found” or stale figure numbers) Combined deduction cap is −100%. Citations must meet the source quality standard — see the Citations page . Drop Policies 1 Training Lab grade dropped (lowest of 10) Lab 1.0 and Lab 1.1 are technically droppable, but in practice they aren’t. Lab 1.0 sets up the document mechanics every Engagement Packet depends on, and every lab after 1.1 needs your Kali VM running. Save your drop for a lab that doesn’t gate everything that follows it. 1 Engagement Packet grade dropped (lowest of 5) 1 Module Exam grade dropped (lowest of 5) star Engagement Packet Bonus (Tier 3) Up to +10% for work that exceeds the spec. Examples: a non-required tool documented to runbook standard, a finding that shows analyst-level judgment beyond what the lab scenario requires, or documentation craftsmanship that materially improves the deliverable. Bonuses are awarded sparingly and never as compensation for Tier 1 quality gaps. medical_services Think of drops as built-in sick days Just like at work, sick days are not unlimited. Take more than one day at work and it comes out of your check in the form of forfeited wages. Take more than one drop here and it comes out of your GPA in the form of forfeited grades. block Late Work Policy No late work accepted. t: IS3513 - Information Assurance and Security
x: IS3513 Information Assurance & Security UT San Antonio — Fall 2026 — John Newsom New to the course? Complete Start Here first → The Engagement Packet From training to trusted deliverable. The artifact you hand a client — and the one worth showing in an interview. Every module at NEXUS ends the way real consulting work does: with something you hand to a client. The Engagement Packet is where your reconnaissance, analysis, and testing stops being scratch work and becomes a professional record — an internal runbook the next analyst can follow, and a client-ready report that stands on its own. Justify your hours, document your process so it’s reproducible, and write findings a non-technical client can act on. See the Engagement Packets → Welcome to IS3513 Welcome to NEXUS Security. You’re the new analyst. A 15-slide tour of how the course works, who you’ll be working with, and what’s due in your first 72 hours. I’m John Newsom. This is Information Assurance and Security. Watch this before you touch a lab — it covers the two questions that drive every assignment in this course, the four Texas clients you’ll work with, how a module is structured, and where to get help. This course is structured as a semester-long consulting engagement. You’re a Junior Analyst at NEXUS Security , a fictional Texas-based cybersecurity consulting firm. Over five modules you’ll work four real-world client engagements — Brazos Financial, Gulf Coast Healthcare, Alamo Industries, and LoneStar DevOps — spanning the full breadth of analyst work: reconnaissance, cryptography, network analysis, threat assessment, and risk management. t: How To Get Help
x: how to get help Support Resources & Channels Stuck on a lab? Confused about a concept? Need an extension? Here’s how to get help. Pick the right tool for the situation : Public questions (technical, conceptual, “how does this work”) → AI first, Discord second. Personal asks (extensions, accommodations, grades, anything tied to your specific situation) → Email from your UT San Antonio account, always. Step 1 AI Tools Step 2 Discord Step 3 Calendly Step 4 Email Step 5 Drop-In Zoom lock The FERPA Rule Don’t put personal information on Discord. Discord is a third-party platform UT San Antonio doesn’t control. Grades, student IDs, personal circumstances, family information, medical or accommodation details — none of that goes on Discord, not even in a DM to me. Use your UT San Antonio email ( john.newsom@utsa.edu ) for anything that touches PII. This protects both of us. 1. Try AI First (For Syntax & Concepts) If your question is “what does this flag do?” or “why am I getting this error?” or “what does this concept mean?” — ask an AI tool first. ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot are excellent for syntax, error messages, and concept explanations. You’ll usually get an answer in seconds. Verify what AI tells you against tool documentation, man pages, or the textbook. See the GenAI Policy for what AI can and can’t help with. AI is best for: Command syntax and flag explanations Decoding cryptic error messages Concept clarification (“explain ARP poisoning like I’m 12”) Proofreading your writing AI is NOT best for: course-specific questions (“do I need to cite this?”), policy questions (“can I get an extension?”), or anything that depends on context AI can’t see. Those go to Discord or email. 2. Ask on Discord (Fastest Response from Humans) When AI can’t help — or when you need a human who knows the course — Discord is the fastest path. Classmates, course alumni, and the instructor monitor the channels; questions usually get answered within a few hours. Pick the right channel: #module-1-help through #module-5-help — lab technical questions for that specific module #course-questions — policy, deadlines, grading questions #technical-questions — general technical questions not tied to a specific module #tools-and-resources — sharing useful tools, cheat sheets, finds When asking questions: Describe what you’re trying to do. Share the error message in a code block. Include a screenshot if relevant — but use a real screen capture, not a phone photo of your monitor . Phone photos look unprofessional and are hard to read. Every OS has built-in screen-snipping tools (Windows: Win+Shift+S ; macOS: Cmd+Shift+4 ); if you don’t know how to use them, AI does and will walk you through it. You need to know how to make clean screen captures anyway — you’ll use them in every Engagement Packet. Bring the same professional respect to your colleagues that you do to your clients. Be specific — “it doesn’t work” doesn’t help us help you. View Discord Info → forum Post in public channels — not DMs. The whole point of the Discord server is peer learning. If you have a question, other students probably have it too. Asking in public means three things happen: you might get an answer from a classmate or alumnus faster than from me; everyone else with the same question gets the answer too; and the answer stays searchable for the next person who hits the same problem. Here’s how I work the server so you can read the signals right: when a classmate gives the right answer, I’ll react with a 👍 or drop a short reply (“exactly,” “that’s it”). When a peer answer is wrong or incomplete, I jump in and correct it. My reaction or reply means I’ve seen the thread and the answer is endorsed — silence isn’t disapproval, but it’s also not endorsement yet. I check Discord frequently during the day, less so at night — I’m not a 24/7 lurker. If you post at 2 a.m., expect that I might not see it until the next afternoon. Give classmates a couple of hours to answer before DMing me directly. If you posted a question and 24 hours later you don’t see a peer response and don’t see an instructor reaction, ping me with @ProfessorNewsom in the channel or shoot me an email. I’m not ignoring you — the thread got lost, and a nudge fixes it fast. 3. Book an Appointment (One-on-One Help) Need dedicated one-on-one time? Book an appointment through Calendly. You pick the format, in person or online, and the length: 15, 30, 45, or 60 minutes. Great for complex debugging, career questions, or anything that needs focused attention. Format: In person or online, your choice when you book. This is an asynchronous course, so there are no fixed office hours, but Calendly is open for scheduled appointments throughout the term. Book Appointment → 4. Email the Instructor (Private Matters Only) Email is the only channel for anything personal: grade questions, accommodations, extension requests, personal circumstances, or anything tied to your specific situation. Use your UT San Antonio email — not a personal Gmail/Yahoo/Hotmail account. If you email me from a personal account, the only response you’ll get is “Please resend this email from your student account.” FERPA only allows me to discuss personal matters over services owned by UT San Antonio — I cannot send an email about your record to a personal address. Emails on the UT San Antonio server are also archived, which protects both of us. Help me help you. Lead every email with this information: Subject: IS3513 §[section] — [brief topic] Body opener: My name is [name], abc123, IS3513 §[section]. I teach multiple courses with multiple sections, and emails that make me dig through five rosters to figure out who you are and what class you’re in get answered slower. If you’re asking for something — an extension, an exception, a recommendation — I’m also less inclined to grant it when the request shows up without context. The two seconds it takes to add this information buys you a faster, friendlier response. Response time: Within 24 hours Mon–Fri. Weekend or holiday emails: next business day. john.newsom@utsa.edu Response time: Within 24 hours Mon–Fri. Weekend or holiday emails: next business day. 5. Weekly Drop-In Zoom (Open Office Hours) Once a week I host an open Zoom for anyone who wants to ask something live. It’s not course-specific and it’s not private — think of it as walk-in office hours over Zoom. No appointment needed; just show up. When: Tuesdays at 6:00 p.m. CT , every week of the term — starting the first week of classes. How it works: I open the Zoom room at the scheduled time. If no one joins in the first five minutes, I close the room and move on with my day. If you show up, we talk. Not recorded. Nothing is posted afterward. This is a real-time channel only. Personal/FERPA-touching questions still belong in email, not the open Zoom — anyone could be in the room. Join Drop-In Zoom → do_not_disturb Please Don’t DM me on Discord before posting publicly — you’re cutting off the peer-learning loop the server exists for. Email me from a personal Gmail/Yahoo/Hotmail account — you’ll just get redirected back to UT San Antonio email anyway. Email questions about command syntax or error messages — those get faster answers in the public Discord channels. Wait until the night before a deadline to ask for help. AI, Discord, Calendly, email, and the weekly drop-in Zoom cover everything you need.

t: NEXUS Security
x: nexus security San Antonio, Texas · Boutique Cybersecurity Consulting waving_hand Welcome to NEXUS Security You’ve just been hired as a Junior Security Analyst . NEXUS specializes in helping Texas businesses understand and improve their security posture. Your first day starts now. How Engagements Work Every module follows the same consulting workflow. Internal training first, then a client engagement at the end. Labs X.1 and X.2: Training Labs (Internal Training): Before touching a client system, you train on NEXUS’s methodology. Senior analysts guide you through tools, techniques, and documentation standards. Engagement Packet (Client Engagement): You’re on the clock. Apply your training to a real client’s systems, document your findings, and deliver a professional report that goes to executives. Deliverable — Engagement Packet: One .docx file, two parts. Part I (Internal Packet): Timesheet + Runbook + Reflection. Part II (Client Deliverable): Cover, Executive Summary, Findings, Risk Analysis, Recommendations. The client only sees Part II. See the Engagement Packet Guide for details. Red Team, Blue Team, Purple Team Real security work demands both offensive and defensive perspectives. Red team thinking is the attacker’s mindset — what could go wrong, how would they get in, where are the gaps. Blue team thinking is the defender’s — what controls catch this, how do we detect, how do we respond. The course rotates you through both. Modules 2 and 5 sit in the middle — the purple team zone where you find the weakness AND recommend the fix. That’s the consulting sweet spot. Red Team Thinking Modules 1 & 4 — you operate from the attacker’s side. How would an attacker approach this target? What attack surface is exposed? What’s exploitable? What’s the path from the outside in to the crown jewels? Blue Team Thinking Module 3 — you operate from the defender’s side. How do we detect this attack in the logs? How do we prevent it before it succeeds? What controls actually work against a real adversary? Your Responsibilities as a Junior Analyst Track Your Time: Every hour is billable — internal training or client work. Your timesheet justifies NEXUS’s invoices. Document Everything: If it’s not documented, it didn’t happen. Your runbooks help the next analyst; your reports go to executives. Communicate Professionally: Clients aren’t always technical. Translate findings into business impact and make recommendations actionable. Learn Continuously: Every module builds on the last. Skills compound. By the end, you’ll have a portfolio of five professional engagement packets. Meet Your Team → Meet Your Clients → Head to Module 1 and begin your training with Lab 1.1 . Your first client is waiting.

t: Scoring Your Findings
x: scoring your findings CVSS, the Risk Matrix, and Why the Two Don’t Always Agree You’ve finished Lab 5.1. You have your top 10 vulnerabilities on LoneStar DevOps — now you’re staring at the Findings and Risk Analysis sections wondering how to turn “I found a thing” into a defensible score. Here’s the one idea to hold onto: every finding gets two different numbers, and they answer two different questions. Most of the confusion comes from treating them as the same number. They’re not. The Two Scores You’re Producing CVSS doesn’t know anything about LoneStar. It doesn’t know they’re prepping a Series B, doesn’t know the MySQL box holds every customer’s credentials, doesn’t know the portal can’t go offline during business hours. That context-free consistency is its strength — an analyst in San Antonio and a vendor in Berlin score the same bug the same way. The risk score is the opposite: it exists entirely to bring LoneStar’s context back in. A scanner can hand you CVSS. Only you can tell Amanda what it means for her. Score What it measures Where it lives CVSS base score How dangerous the vulnerability is in the abstract — regardless of who owns the system. A standardized, client-independent number. Severity rating on each Finding Risk score (Likelihood × Impact) How much the vulnerability actually threatens LoneStar specifically , given their business, assets, and exposure. Risk Analysis section & 5×5 matrix lightbulb The whole point When these two scores disagree , that disagreement is the most valuable thing in your report. A high-CVSS bug on a throwaway asset and a mid-CVSS bug on the crown jewels is exactly the judgment a client pays a consultant for. Part 3 is where that pays off. Part 1 · CVSS 3.1 — Scoring the Vulnerability Itself Score every finding with the official FIRST CVSS 3.1 calculator: first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1 . There are two ways to get a score. If the CVE already has one — most of your WordPress, Apache, PHP, and dependency findings will — look it up on the NVD and read its published 3.1 vector, but still understand why each metric was set that way, because you’ll defend it to the client. {w('If there is no single CVE')} — default credentials, a former employee’s account left active, a misconfiguration — you walk the calculator yourself from the vulnerability’s real characteristics. Pitfall: a lot of older CVE entries show a CVSS 2.0 score, which doesn’t line up with 3.1. Always score on the 3.1 calculator so the whole class is comparable. The Eight Base Metrics, in Plain Language You’re answering eight small, concrete questions. Don’t overthink them. Attack Vector (AV) — where must the attacker be? Network → Adjacent → Local → Physical. Closer required = lower score. Attack Complexity (AC) — how hard is the exploit, beyond the attacker’s control? Low = fire it off reliably; High = needs a race condition or special setup. Privileges Required (PR) — what access do they need first ? None / Low / High. Default credentials are the classic PR:None — the door’s already unlocked. User Interaction (UI) — does a victim have to do something (click a link)? None, or Required. Required lowers the score. Scope (S) — can the blast escape its own security boundary? Unchanged, or Changed. Scope:Changed is the single biggest score multiplier — use it carefully. Confidentiality / Integrity / Availability (C / I / A) — what does a successful attack cost? None / Low / High each. Read data = C, alter data = I, take it down = A. The classic mix-up: Attack Vector is where the attacker stands ; Attack Complexity is how hard the exploit is once they’re there . Different axes. From Score to Severity The calculator returns a number from 0.0 to 10.0, which maps to the severity label you write on the Finding. These are the official FIRST CVSS 3.1 bands: CVSS base score Severity 9.0 – 10.0 Critical 7.0 – 8.9 High 4.0 – 6.9 Medium 0.1 – 3.9 Low 0.0 None / Informational Carry two things into the report for every finding. First, the vector string the calculator produces — it’s the receipt that lets anyone reconstruct your number. Second, one sentence of rationale for why you set the metrics that way. A score with no explanation is just a number, and a number nobody can defend is worth nothing to a client. Worked Example — the Mechanics Say you found an unauthenticated remote code execution on a service reachable over the network, no special conditions, no victim action, that fully compromises the box. Walk the metrics: AV Network, AC Low, PR None, UI None, Scope Unchanged, C/I/A High/High/High. CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H → 9.8, Critical That’s the textbook worst case. Every one of your findings is a step down from it — an attacker who needs local access first (AV:L), a bug that only leaks data (I:N), a flaw that needs a click (UI:R). Move the metrics to match reality and let the calculator do the arithmetic. Part 2 · The 5×5 Risk Matrix — Scoring the Risk to LoneStar Now switch hats — CVSS is done. You’re building a 5×5 grid : every finding gets a Likelihood (1–5) and an Impact (1–5), and Risk = Likelihood × Impact . This is where LoneStar’s world comes back into the picture. Likelihood — how probable is exploitation, here? 1 2 3 4 5 Rare Unlikely Possible Likely Almost Certain Reason it out: Is the thing exposed to the internet or buried on an internal segment? Does working exploit code already exist? Does the attacker need credentials or local access first (which lowers likelihood)? Is it something bots scan for around the clock — default creds, exposed admin panels are Likely-to-Almost-Certain. Impact — what does it cost LoneStar if it happens? 1 2 3 4 5 Negligible Minor Moderate Major Catastrophic Here you must think in LoneStar’s specifics, not generic severity. $12M ARR, 200+ customers, Series B in due diligence. A breach that surfaces during investor due diligence doesn’t just cost data — it can cost the round. Customer credentials and API keys live in the database. Anything touching that asset is a candidate for Major or Catastrophic — the blast radius is every customer. The customer portal is the business. Availability hits there are far worse than the same downtime on an internal dev box. Two findings with identical CVSS can land on completely different Impact rows purely because of which asset they touch. That’s correct — that’s the point of the section. Risk Score and Bands Multiply Likelihood by Impact, then color-code onto the grid: Risk = Likelihood × Impact Band 15 – 25 Critical 10 – 14 High 5 – 9 Medium 1 – 4 Low Plot all 10 findings on the 5×5 grid. That visual is what Amanda actually reads — executives grasp “top-right red quadrant” far faster than “CVSS 9.8.” Translating the technical into the visual-and-business is the whole job of this section. Part 3 · CVSS ≠ Business Priority Here’s the payoff of producing two scores instead of one. They will sometimes disagree, and when they do, business risk wins — as long as you explain why. The CVSS numbers below are illustrative (yours come from your own calculator runs), but the reasoning is exactly what your report has to show: Finding CVSS (illustrative) Real priority Why they diverge MySQL default root credentials ~7.3 (High) Highest Lower CVSS, but it exposes every customer’s data — the crown-jewel asset for a company in Series B due diligence. WordPress SQL injection 9.8 (Critical) High, not top Huge CVSS, but it sits on the public marketing / WordPress surface, not the customer data store. Apache privilege-escalation CVE ~7.8 (High) Medium Dangerous once you are already on the box — needs local access first, so real-world likelihood is lower. SSH weak passwords ~8.8 (High) High Administrative-access risk — crackable credentials on accounts that can touch production. Look at the top two rows: the vulnerability with the lower CVSS is the higher business priority. Rank purely by CVSS and you’d hand Amanda a report that puts the marketing-site bug above the one that leaks her entire customer base — and she’d be right to fire NEXUS over it. A high CVSS on a low-value or isolated asset is lower business risk than the raw number suggests (public WordPress SQLi). A moderate CVSS on the crown-jewel asset is higher business risk than the raw number suggests (MySQL default creds on the customer database). What’s reachable from the internet, what data an asset holds, and what breaks if it’s compromised all move business risk up or down independently of CVSS. Priority isn’t only about risk — it’s about what LoneStar can do . When you sequence remediation, weigh remediation complexity and their real constraints: a 2-person DevOps team (Sarah and Miguel), no staging environment, a zero-downtime customer portal, and a 4-week window before the enterprise review. Lead with quick wins (disable the former-employee account, change the default MySQL password, rotate exposed API keys) so Sarah has something to show Amanda next unit. Before You Export — Make Your Scores Agree With Themselves Your two scores are allowed to point different directions — that’s Part 3 — but they have to be internally consistent and explained. This is the easiest way to throw away points you already earned: The severity label on a Finding must match the CVSS score you gave it. Don’t call something “Critical” in Findings and score it 6.4. Your Risk Analysis rating may differ from raw CVSS — but only if you say why , in LoneStar’s terms. That “why” is the entire section. The single most common way to lose Risk Analysis points is a uniform “high risk” on all ten findings with no reasoning. Differentiate them — each finding gets its own “so what?” for Amanda. A given finding must carry the same severity everywhere it appears — Findings, Risk Analysis, and Executive Summary. Ratings that drift between sections read as carelessness. verified The bar A report where every finding has a defensible CVSS vector, a differentiated likelihood-and-impact reasoned through LoneStar’s business, and a priority order that reflects business risk rather than raw CVSS — that’s the actual job of a security consultant. That’s what EP 5 is testing. Quick Reference CVSS 3.1 bands: 9.0–10.0 Critical · 7.0–8.9 High · 4.0–6.9 Medium · 0.1–3.9 Low · 0.0 None/Informational Likelihood (1–5): Rare · Unlikely · Possible · Likely · Almost Certain Impact (1–5): Negligible · Minor · Moderate · Major · Catastrophic Risk = Likelihood × Impact: 15–25 Critical · 10–14 High · 5–9 Medium · 1–4 Low Sources Worth Citing All of these meet the source-quality standard — use them in-text where they support a score or a rating: FIRST — CVSS v3.1 Specification & Calculator: first.org/cvss/specification-document NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD): nvd.nist.gov NIST SP 800-30 — Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments (the likelihood × impact methodology) NIST SP 800-115 — Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment OWASP Risk Rating Methodology Still stuck on a specific finding? Bring it to the Tuesday drop-in Zoom (6:00 p.m. CT) or post it in #module-5-help — paste your metric selections and your reasoning, and we’ll work it live.

t: Screenshot Requirements
x: screenshot requirements Evidence Standards for Lab Submissions Screenshots are evidence . In professional security work, undocumented claims don’t exist. Every screenshot must prove you did the work on your system. error Deduction −2.5% per qualifying screenshot short of 20. Twenty qualifying screenshots from a module’s labs earns full screenshot credit; more than 20 earns nothing extra unless a screenshot is your evidence for a stretch goal. A qualifying screenshot is readable, comes from this module’s labs, shows your abc123 (in the terminal prompt, or in the title bar of the full Kali VM window), and sits inline in the .docx next to the text that references it. Duplicates count once. A documented failure you captured and explained counts. Combined with other documentation deductions, the cap is −100%. ✓ Verifiable Screenshot abc123 in terminal prompt — kali㉿<your abc123> visible abc123 in window title bar — the full Kali VM window, title bar included Hostname visible in command output — e.g., uname -n output ✗ Unverifiable Screenshot Default "kali@kali" prompt — hostname never changed to your abc123 Cropped to hide hostname — partial screenshots rejected Web browser only, no VM context — could be anyone’s machine Critical: VM Name Visibility Name your VM <your abc123> and give Kali the same hostname. Your abc123 is the ID you use to log into Canvas (for example, aaa000 ), not your Banner ID number. It then shows in your terminal prompt ( kali㉿aaa000 ) and in the VM window’s title bar. When the prompt can’t show it (inside a container’s SSH session, a browser window, a GUI tool), capture the entire Kali VM window so your abc123 is visible in its title bar. Without your VM name, there’s no way to verify you ran the commands. Screenshots without identification could be copied from anywhere — and occasionally are. Where Each Screenshot Goes Screenshots go inline, inside the .docx, next to the text that references them. Training Lab work (X.1 and X.2) goes in the Runbook, under the entry for the tool that produced it. Client work (the Engagement Packet) goes in Part II, with the finding, methodology step or appendix item it supports. If a runbook entry needs a client screenshot, point to it by figure number with a cross-reference instead of pasting it twice. A screenshot uploaded as a separate file, attached in Canvas or posted as a Canvas comment is not in the packet and does not count. Filename Convention All screenshots follow this naming pattern: ##-description.png 01-hypervisor-recommendation.png — First screenshot, the AI’s hypervisor recommendation 08-nmap-version.png — Eighth screenshot, nmap output 15-wireshark-tcp-stream.png — Fifteenth screenshot, Wireshark analysis Two-digit numbers keep files sorted correctly (01, 02… not 1, 2, 10, 11). This matters when you’re compiling 20+ screenshots into a report. Always Capture Command you ran Output / results VM name visible (terminal prompt or title) Relevant context (IP addresses, tool version, etc.) When Instructed Error messages (document failures too) Configuration screens Before/after comparisons Specific UI elements Folder Organization Keep screenshots organized by lab in your Kali VM: ~/Screenshots/ ├── Lab1-Screenshots/ │ ├── 01-hypervisor-recommendation.png │ ├── 02-vm-settings.png │ └── ... ├── Lab2-Screenshots/ ├── Lab3-Screenshots/ └── ... lightbulb Pro Tip Screenshot as you go. Don’t try to recreate screenshots after the fact. Take them in real-time as you work. Missing a screenshot means redoing the work — or taking the deduction. Every screenshot is evidence. Make it count.

routing) Layer 2 — Data Link (MAC addresses, switches) Layer 1 — Physical (cables, hubs) TCP vs. UDP TCP — connection-oriented, reliable, three-way handshake (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK) UDP — connectionless, unreliable, no handshake, faster TCP ports — HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), SSH (22), FTP (21), Telnet (23), SMTP (25) UDP ports — DNS (53), DHCP (67/68), TFTP (69), SNMP (161) Network Protocols ICMP — Internet Control Message Protocol, used by ping and traceroute ARP — Address Resolution Protocol, maps IP to MAC addresses DHCP — Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, assigns IP addresses DNS — Domain Name System, resolves names to IP addresses SLAAC — Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, IPv6 auto-config IP Addressing IPv4 — 32 bits, dotted decimal (192.168.1.1) IPv6 — 128 bits, hexadecimal with Class B — /16, 65,534 hosts Class C — /24, 254 hosts 2 Network Devices What lives at Layers 1, 2, and 3 Layer 1 Devices Hub — broadcasts to all ports, shared collision domain Repeater — regenerates signal to extend distance Layer 2 Devices Switch — forwards based on MAC address, separate collision domains per port Bridge — connects network segments at Layer 2 WAP (Wireless Access Point) — connects wireless clients to wired network Layer 3 Devices Router — forwards based on IP address, separates broadcast domains Layer 3 switch — switch with routing capabilities Security Devices Firewall — filters traffic based on rules IDS (Intrusion Detection System) — monitors and alerts IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) — monitors and blocks Proxy — intermediary that filters/caches traffic Load balancer — distributes traffic across servers VPN concentrator — handles VPN connections 3 Network Architecture Topologies, zones, and segmentation Network Types LAN — Local Area Network, single location WAN — Wide Area Network, geographically dispersed WLAN — Wireless LAN MAN — Metropolitan Area Network PAN — Personal Area Network (Bluetooth) Network Zones Intranet — internal network, trusted zone Extranet — extended access to partners DMZ — Demilitarized Zone, buffer between internal and external Internet — public, untrusted network Topologies Star — all devices connect to central point (most common) Bus — single cable, all devices attached Ring — devices connected in a circle Mesh — every device connected to every other device Hybrid — combination of topologies Segmentation VLAN — Virtual LAN, logical segmentation Subnetting — dividing networks into smaller segments NAT — Network Address Translation, hides internal IPs PAT — Port Address Translation, multiple internal IPs share one external Air gap — complete physical isolation 4 Intrusion Detection & Prevention How IDS/IPS systems see attacks coming IDS Types NIDS — Network-based, monitors network traffic HIDS — Host-based, monitors single system (files, processes, logs) Wireless IDS — monitors wireless networks Detection Methods Signature-based — compares against known attack patterns (signature database) Anomaly-based — compares against baseline of normal behavior Heuristic — uses rules and algorithms to identify suspicious activity IDS Outcomes True positive — correctly identified attack True negative — correctly identified normal traffic False positive — alert on legitimate traffic (not actually malicious) False negative — missed actual attack (malicious goes undetected) IDS/IPS Tools Snort — open-source IDS since 1998, de facto standard Suricata — high-performance alternative to Snort OSSEC — host-based IDS Zeek (formerly Bro) — network analysis framework Key Concepts Promiscuous mode — NIC captures all traffic, not just addressed to it Inline vs. passive — IPS inline (can block), IDS passive (monitor only) Correlation — connecting related events from multiple sources SIEM — Security Information and Event Management Encrypted traffic limitation — NIDS cannot inspect encrypted payloads 5 Cloud & Virtualization Service models, deployment models, and the shared responsibility line Cloud Service Models IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service (VMs, storage, networking) PaaS — Platform as a Service (development environment) SaaS — Software as a Service (applications via browser) XaaS — Anything as a Service Cloud Deployment Models Public cloud — shared infrastructure, third-party operated Private cloud — dedicated to single organization Hybrid cloud — combination Core Risk Concepts Risk — possibility of suffering harm or loss Threat — potential cause of unwanted incident Vulnerability — weakness that can be exploited Asset — anything of value to organization Impact — actual damage when threat exploits vulnerability Likelihood — probability threat will exploit vulnerability Attack vector — path attacker uses to reach target Threat vector — method threat uses to gain access Risk Relationships Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact or simplified: Risk = Likelihood × Impact Risk Truths Risk cannot be completely eliminated — it’s absolute Not every risk needs to be mitigated Risk management must balance cost vs. benefit Qualitative and quantitative approaches both have value 2 Quantitative Risk Analysis ALE, SLE, ARO, and the math that drives risk decisions Key Formulas SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) = AV × EF ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) = SLE × ARO AV = Asset Value EF = Exposure Factor (percentage of asset lost) ARO = Annualized Rate of Occurrence Quantitative Metrics TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) — all costs over asset lifetime ROI (Return on Investment) — benefit vs. cost ratio MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) — average time before failure MTTR (Mean Time to Repair) — average time to restore RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — maximum acceptable downtime RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — maximum acceptable data loss Practice Problem A server farm has 5 servers. If 2 fail in an incident, what is the Exposure Factor? identified risks Risk owner — person accountable for managing specific risk Risk appetite — level of risk organization willing to accept Risk tolerance — acceptable deviation from risk appetite Residual risk — risk remaining after controls implemented Inherent risk — risk before any controls 4 Risk Treatment Strategies Mitigate, transfer, accept, avoid — and when each applies The Four
